title: PLINK for Livestock Genomics
text:
Welcome
I wrote this tutorial because most PLINK material is written for human genetics. The ideas are the same in cattle, sheep and goats, but the details are not: we have 29 cattle autosomes instead of 22, we have big half-sib families, we mix breeds, and our pedigrees are often wrong. Every example here uses livestock data, and every PLINK output you see was produced by actually running the command shown. The few commands for other programs that could not be installed where this book was built (BEAGLE, SHAPEIT, Minimac, GCTA, GEMMA) are clearly marked as not run.

title: PLINK for Livestock Genomics
text:
The data
We use two kinds of data.
A simulated cattle dataset (361 animals of three breeds, 4,800 SNPs). Because it was simulated, we know the truth: I hid lab errors (bad samples, a duplicate, a wrong sire, sex mix-ups, strand flips) and real genetic effects in it, and the chapters show how PLINK finds each one.
Two real public datasets: 500 genotyped cattle with a pedigree (from the synbreedData R package) and 100 sheep of two breeds, Jacob and Navajo-Churro, published by Kijas and colleagues (2016) and shipped with the detectRUNS R package. These show what real data look like, which is always a little messier than a simulation.
Everything is in the data/ and scripts/ folders of the GitHub repository, so you can repeat every step.

title: PLINK for Livestock Genomics
text:
Which PLINK?
PLINK has three versions that are still in use. This book uses PLINK 1.9 for almost everything, gives the PLINK 2.0 command in a blue box, and uses PLINK 1.07 only for the old tools that newer versions dropped (haplotype tests and CNV analysis). Chapter 1 explains the differences.

title: 1  Installing PLINK and running your first command
text:
1.1 What PLINK is
Picture a giant spreadsheet. Each row is an animal, each column is a SNP, and each cell holds two letters, one inherited from the sire and one from the dam (for example A G). A 50K chip gives 50,000 columns; a high-density chip gives 777,000. No spreadsheet program can open that. PLINK can. It reads the genotypes, checks their quality, counts things, compares groups of animals and writes small result tables that you can open in R or Excel.

section: 1.4 Step 2: unzip and put it somewhere sensible
text:
1.4 Step 2: unzip and put it somewhere sensible
Create one folder for your genomics work, for example C:/genomics on Windows or ~/genomics on macOS and Linux, and unzip PLINK there. Put your data in the same folder at first. Later, when you are comfortable, you can add PLINK to your PATH so that it runs from any folder.

WindowsmacOSLinuxLinux or macOS with conda



Unzip the file into C:\genomics.
Open Command Prompt (press the Windows key, type cmd, press Enter).
Move into your folder and test PLINK:

cd C:\genomics
plink --version
To run PLINK from any folder, add C:\genomics to your PATH: search for “Edit the system environment variables”, click Environment Variables, select Path, click Edit, then New, and paste C:\genomics.



Unzip the file into ~/genomics (a folder called genomics in your home folder).
Open Terminal (Applications, Utilities).
Make the file executable and test it:

cd ~/genomics
chmod +x plink
./plink --version
The first time, macOS may refuse to open a program from an “unidentified developer”. Either right-click the file in Finder and choose Open, or run xattr -d com.apple.quarantine plink once in the terminal.


mkdir -p ~/genomics && cd ~/genomics
unzip plink_linux_x86_64_*.zip
chmod +x plink
./plink --version
# optional: make it available everywhere
sudo cp plink /usr/local/bin/


If you already use conda (Miniconda, Anaconda, Miniforge or micromamba), the Bioconda channel has ready-made packages called plink (PLINK 1.9) and plink2. Conda puts the programs on your PATH inside the environment, so you do not have to unzip anything or run chmod.
# 1. once only: tell conda where to look (Bioconda needs conda-forge)
conda config --add channels bioconda
conda config --add channels conda-forge
conda config --set channel_priority strict

# 2. a separate environment for this course, with both versions
conda create -n plink_course plink plink2
conda activate plink_course

# 3. check
plink --version
plink2 --version
which plink          # e.g. /home/you/miniforge3/envs/plink_course/bin/plink
Things to know:

Run conda activate plink_course in every new terminal before using PLINK; otherwise plink: command not found.
mamba or micromamba accept the same commands and solve environments faster.
Bioconda’s builds can lag behind the newest PLINK 2.0 build on the official page. If a flag from the PLINK 2.0 documentation is missing, compare plink2 --version with the date on the website and download the newer build by hand.
The Bioconda plink package is PLINK 1.9. For PLINK 1.07 (Chapters 14 and 15), download it by hand as above.
On Windows, use the zip download (or conda inside WSL, the Windows Subsystem for Linux).




If you see a line such as PLINK v1.9..., you are ready. On macOS and Linux, ./plink means “the plink in this folder”. Once PLINK is on your PATH, you can type just plink.

title: 1  Installing PLINK and running your first command
text:
1.6 Anatomy of a PLINK command
Every PLINK command has three parts: what to read, what to do, and where to write.
plink --bfile cattle --cow --geno 0.05 --make-bed --out cattle_clean
#      \___ read ___/ \_______ do ________/ \___ write ___/

--bfile cattle reads the three files cattle.bed, cattle.bim and cattle.fam. You give the name without the extension.
Words starting with two dashes are flags. Some take a value (--geno 0.05); some do not (--cow).
--out cattle_clean sets the start of every output file name. Without it, PLINK calls everything plink.* and overwrites your earlier results.
The order of flags on the line does not matter. PLINK decides the order of operations itself (Chapter 6 shows why this matters).

title: 1  Installing PLINK and running your first command
section: 1.7 The log file is your best friend
text:
1.7 The log file is your best friend
Every run writes a .log file with the same name as the output (cattle_clean.log). It repeats your command and reports what happened: how many animals and SNPs were read, how many were removed and why, and any warnings. Get into the habit of reading it every time. PLINK usually does exactly what you asked, which is not always what you meant, and the log is where you find out.

title: 1  Installing PLINK and running your first command
section: 1.8 The flag every livestock user needs: --cow
text:
1.8 The flag every livestock user needs: --cow
PLINK was written for humans. By default it expects chromosomes 1 to 22, and it reads code 23 as X, 24 as Y, 25 as the pseudo-autosomal region (XY) and 26 as mitochondria. Cattle have 29 autosomes. This is what happened when I loaded our cattle file without telling PLINK the species:
Error: Invalid chromosome code '27' on line 4101 of .map file.
(This is disallowed for humans.  Check if the problem is with your data, or if
you forgot to define a different chromosome set with e.g. --chr-set.)
That error is the lucky case. If your file only had chromosomes up to 26, PLINK would have read cattle chromosome 23 as the X and chromosome 24 as the Y without complaining, and your sex checks and association results would be quietly wrong.

title: 2  Using PLINK from R and RStudio
text:
2.1 Step 1: install R, RStudio and a few packages
There is no “PLINK package” that replaces the PLINK program. In R we do one of two things: we call the PLINK program from R, or we read PLINK’s files into R. This chapter shows both.

Use File > New Project > New Directory, call it plink_tutorial, and put the PLINK program and the practice data in that folder. A project sets the working directory for you, so you never need setwd() with a long path that only works on your own computer.
plink_tutorial/

title: 2  Using PLINK from R and RStudio
section: 2.3 Step 3: get PLINK into the project
text:
2.3 Step 3: get PLINK into the project
You have three choices. Use whichever works on your computer.
Option A: download it by hand (Chapter 1) and copy the file into the project folder.
Option B: let R download it. The bigsnpr package has helper functions that download the right PLINK build for your system and return its path:
library(bigsnpr)
plink  <- download_plink(dir = ".")     # PLINK 1.9
plink2 <- download_plink2(dir = ".")    # PLINK 2.0
plink                                    # prints the full path, e.g. "./plink"
Option C: use the RStudio Terminal. RStudio has a Terminal tab next to the Console. It is a normal command line that opens in your project folder, so every command in this book works there unchanged.
crumbs: 2  Using PLINK from R and RStudio

title: 2  Using PLINK from R and RStudio
text:
2.4 Step 4: run PLINK from R
R’s system2() function runs an outside program. Give it the program path and the arguments:
plink <- "./plink"           # on Windows: "plink.exe"

system2(plink, args = c("--file", "data/cattle", "--cow",
                        "--make-bed", "--out", "results/cattle"))
The older system() function takes the whole command as one string, which is handy for copying commands from this book:
system("./plink --bfile results/cattle --cow --missing --out results/miss")

2.4.1 A complete script with system()
Many people keep their whole analysis in one R script built around system(). Here is a typical one, written for the files of this book:
# clear the workspace (removes your R objects; loaded packages stay loaded)
rm(list = ls())

# set the working directory: the folder that holds PLINK and the data
setwd("D:/genomics/plink_tutorial")        # Windows
# setwd("~/genomics/plink_tutorial")       # macOS or Linux

# run PLINK: read the binary files, convert them back to text
system("plink --bfile cattle --cow --nonfounders --allow-no-sex --recode --out cattle_QC_out")
What each part of the PLINK command does, and what it printed when we ran it:







Part
Meaning




plink
The program. This works only if PLINK is on your PATH (Chapter 1). Otherwise give the path: "./plink ..." on macOS and Linux, "plink.exe ..." or "D:/genomics/plink.exe ..." on Windows


--bfile cattle
Read cattle.bed, cattle.bim and cattle.fam from the working directory


--cow
29 cattle autosomes plus X, Y and MT


--nonfounders
Count all 361 animals, not only the 301 founders, when PLINK computes allele frequencies


--allow-no-sex
Keep the phenotypes of the two animals with unknown sex


--recode
Write text files: cattle_QC_out.ped and .map


--out cattle_QC_out
Start of every output file name



4800 variants loaded from .bim file.
361 cattle (137 males, 222 females, 2 ambiguous) loaded from .fam.
Before main variant filters, 301 founders and 60 nonfounders present.
Calculating allele frequencies... done.
Total genotyping rate is 0.992812.
4800 variants and 361 cattle pass filters and QC.
--recode ped to cattle_QC_out.ped + cattle_QC_out.map ... done.
It worked, but two things are worth knowing. First, this command does no QC at all: --recode only converts, and nothing was removed (4,800 SNPs and 361 animals in, the same out). Give the output a name that says what it is, such as cattle_text. Second, --nonfounders changes nothing you can see here. It only matters where PLINK computes allele frequencies: in --freq, --hardy, --maf and --hwe, and when it decides which allele is the minor one (A1). For example, --freq gave snp00001 a MAF of 0.0249 from the 301 founders (602 chromosomes) and 0.0292 with --nonfounders (720 chromosomes). Add a flag only when you know which step it changes.
Two R details. system() returns PLINK’s exit status: 0 means success, anything else means PLINK stopped with an error, so status <- system("plink ...") followed by if (status != 0) stop("PLINK failed") stops a long script at the first problem. And setwd() with a full path ties the script to one computer; an RStudio project (Step 2) avoids that. (The PLINK output above is real; R itself was not available where this book was built, so the R lines are shown, not run.)
On Windows, write paths with forward slashes ("C:/genomics/plink.exe") or doubled backslashes ("C:\\genomics\\plink.exe"). A single backslash breaks the string.
A small helper function saves typing and prints PLINK’s messages in the Console:
run_plink <- function(..., exe = "./plink") {
  args <- c(...)
  out <- system2(exe, args = args, stdout = TRUE, stderr = TRUE)
  cat(out, sep = "\n")
  invisible(out)
}

run_plink("--bfile", "results/cattle", "--cow", "--freq", "--out", "results/freq")

section: 2.5 Step 5: read the results into R
text:
2.5 Step 5: read the results into R
Almost every PLINK output is a plain text table with a header line and columns separated by spaces. read.table(header = TRUE) reads it, and data.table::fread() does the same faster for big files.
library(tidyverse)

imiss <- read.table("results/miss.imiss", header = TRUE)
lmiss <- read.table("results/miss.lmiss", header = TRUE)

ggplot(imiss, aes(x = F_MISS * 100)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "#E69F00") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Missing genotypes per animal (%)", y = "Number of animals",
       title = "Missingness per animal") +
  theme_minimal()







PLINK output
How to read it in R




.frq, .hwe, .imiss, .lmiss, .het, .genome, .assoc, .qassoc, .assoc.linear
read.table(file, header = TRUE)


.eigenvec written with --pca header
read.table(file, header = TRUE)


.eigenvec written without header
read.table(file, col.names = c("FID", "IID", paste0("PC", 1:20)))


.eigenval
scan(file) (just a column of numbers)


.mdist, .mibs, .rel (square matrices)
as.matrix(read.table(file))


.raw from --recode A
read.table(file, header = TRUE); genotypes start in column 7


.bed/.bim/.fam themselves
genio::read_plink("results/cattle") or bigsnpr::snp_readBed()



Reading the binary genotypes directly is useful when you want to fit your own models, for example genomic prediction:
library(genio)
geno <- read_plink("results/cattle")
dim(geno$X)        # SNPs in rows, animals in columns, values 0/1/2 or NA
head(geno$bim)     # the SNP map; genio calls A1 "alt" and A2 "ref"
head(geno$fam)     # the animals






WarningWhich allele is being counted?



Different tools count different alleles. genio::read_plink() counts copies of A2 (the allele genio calls ref), while PLINK’s own --recode A file and bigsnpr count copies of A1. For an animal that is A1/A1, genio gives 0 and --recode A gives 2. Before you combine genotypes from two tools, check one SNP by hand.

title: 2  Using PLINK from R and RStudio
section: 2.6 Step 6: let a package do routine QC for you
text:
2.6 Step 6: let a package do routine QC for you
The plinkQC package by Hannah Meyer wraps PLINK’s QC commands (missingness, heterozygosity, sex check, relatedness) and makes clear plots. It follows the QC protocol of Anderson and colleagues (2010).
library(plinkQC)
# 1. run PLINK yourself, with the species flag
system("./plink --bfile results/cattle --cow --missing --out results/cattle")
system("./plink --bfile results/cattle --cow --het --out results/cattle")
# 2. let plinkQC read results/cattle.imiss and results/cattle.het and draw the plot
fail_miss_het <- check_het_and_miss(indir = "results", name = "cattle",
                                     run.check_het_and_miss = FALSE,
                                     imissTh = 0.03, hetTh = 3, interactive = TRUE)
plinkQC was written for human data, and the PLINK commands it runs for you carry no species flag, so on cattle files PLINK would stop at chromosome codes above 26. That is why the example runs PLINK itself with --cow and lets plinkQC only read and plot the results. Every check has a switch for this (run.check_het_and_miss = FALSE above, run.check_sex = FALSE in check_sex()), and it then looks for <name>.imiss, <name>.het or <name>.sexcheck in the folder you give.
crumbs: 2  Using PLINK from R and RStudio

title: 2  Using PLINK from R and RStudio
text:
2.7 Keep a record
Write your commands in an R script or a Quarto notebook rather than typing them into the Console. Six months later, when a reviewer asks “which --geno threshold did you use?”, the answer is in the file, together with the plot it produced.






WarningCommon mistake



If system2() returns status 127 or “cannot find”, R is not looking where PLINK is. Check with file.exists(plink), and on macOS or Linux make the file executable once with Sys.chmod(plink, mode = "0755").

title: 3  Genotype files: what PLINK reads and writes
text:
3.2 The binary format: .bed, .bim and .fam
Text files are huge (each genotype takes four characters: two letters and two spaces) and slow to read. PLINK’s binary format stores each genotype in 2 bits, so our practice file shrank from 6.9 MB to 0.44 MB, and PLINK reads it many times faster. Convert first, and then always work with the binary files.
plink --file cattle --cow --make-bed --out cattle

.fam is the first six columns of the .ped.
.bim is the .map plus two extra columns: allele 1 (A1) and allele 2 (A2).
.bed holds the genotypes. It is not text, so do not open it in an editor.

cattle.bim:  1   snp00001   0.484    484050   G   A
             1   snp00002   2.2237   2223660  C   A






WarningA1 is not “the reference allele”



PLINK 1.9 makes A1 the minor (rarer) allele by default. Every effect size PLINK reports (odds ratio, beta) is for A1. If you need A1 to be a fixed allele, for example the reference allele of the genome assembly, add --keep-allele-order or set it with --a1-allele (Chapter 5). PLINK 2.0 keeps the input order and calls the alleles REF and ALT.

3.3 Other formats you will meet








Format
Files
Typical use




Transposed
.tped + .tfam
One SNP per line; some older programs


Long
.lgen + .map + .fam
One genotype per line; database exports


Additive
.raw from --recode A
0/1/2 counts of A1 per animal; R, Python, genomic prediction

Sequencing tools, imputation (BEAGLE), bcftools

.pgen + .pvar + .psam
Large data and dosages



The additive .raw file is the one you will use most for your own models. Each genotype column counts copies of the allele named in the header:
FID IID PAT MAT SEX PHENOTYPE snp00001_G snp00002_C snp00003_A snp00004_T
ANG ANG_001 0 0 2 1 0 0 0 1
So snp00004_T = 1 means ANG_001 carries one T at that SNP. Missing genotypes appear as NA.

title: 3  Genotype files: what PLINK reads and writes
section: 3.4 Extra files: phenotypes, covariates and clusters
text:
3.4 Extra files: phenotypes, covariates and clusters
Real projects keep traits and covariates in separate files. All of them start with FID and IID:
pheno.txt     FID IID WWT BW YWT BRD
              ANG ANG_001 265.0 38.8 523.1 1
covar.txt     FID IID SEX_M FEEDLOT AGE HERD_N
              ANG ANG_001 0 0 215 1
breed.clst    ANG ANG_001 ANG          (cluster file: no header, third column = group)
You point PLINK to them with --pheno, --covar and --within. Missing values are -9 everywhere unless you change the code with --missing-phenotype.






TipLook before you analyse



head cattle.fam and head cattle.bim take two seconds. Check that sexes are 1 and 2 (not M and F), that phenotypes look sensible, and that chromosome codes are numbers your species flag accepts.

title: 4  The practice data
text:
4.2 The simulated cattle
The cattle were simulated with a Python script (scripts/simulate.py, random seed 2026), so the truth is known. Positions and gene names such as PLAG1 and LCORL are used only as labels to make the story easier to follow; the effects are invented.







Item
What is in the data




Breeds
Angus (ANG), Holstein (HOL), N’Dama (NDA), with different allele frequencies


Animals
361: 240 unrelated (80 per breed), 30 families of sire + dam + 2 calves (15 Holstein, 15 N’Dama), and 1 repeated sample


Sex
137 males, 222 females, 2 unknown


SNPs
4,800: 150 per autosome on chromosomes 1 to 29, extra-dense regions on chromosomes 5, 6 and 14, and 250 on the X


Disease (column 6 of .ped)
BRD, bovine respiratory disease: 144 cases (2), 217 controls (1)


Measured traits (pheno.txt)
WWT weaning weight (kg), BW birth weight (kg), YWT yearling weight (kg)


Covariates (covar.txt)
SEX_M (1 = male), FEEDLOT (1 = feedlot, 0 = pasture), AGE at weaning (days), HERD_N


Other files
batch2 (40 animals genotyped by a second lab), chr14.dosage (imputed dosages), cattle.cnv (CNV calls), genes.txt (regions), breed.clst (breed of each animal)




4.2.1 The hidden problems
These are the things the simulation planted. Try to find them yourself before reading the answer key in Chapter 19.

Some SNPs fail often in the lab, and six animals have poor-quality DNA.
One animal was genotyped twice, and one DNA sample was contaminated with another animal’s DNA.
Two bulls are recorded as cows, and two animals have no recorded sex.
One calf has the wrong sire in the pedigree.
One animal is highly inbred, one is a crossbred and one is labelled with the wrong breed.
Some SNPs have calling errors that break Hardy-Weinberg and Mendel’s laws.
Some SNPs fail more often in sick animals than in healthy ones.
The second lab reported 40 SNPs on the opposite DNA strand.
Real effects: two weaning-weight QTL, one BRD risk SNP, one SNP that only matters in the feedlot, and a CNV deletion linked to BRD.

Simulations are clean. Real data are not, so Chapter 18 repeats the main analyses on two public datasets.

section: 5.2 Step 2: write other formats when another program asks for them
text:
5.2 Step 2: write other formats when another program asks for them
PLINK can write the same genotypes in many layouts. Each one below was made from our binary file with one command of the form plink --bfile cattle --cow <format flag> --out <name>, and each example shows the first lines of what it wrote. Look at your own file the same way (head) before you send it to another program.









Format flag
Files written
Size here
Typical user




--make-bed
.bed .bim .fam
0.44 MB
PLINK, GCTA, ADMIXTURE, most tools


--recode
.ped .map
6.9 MB
Older programs; easy to read


--recode 12
.ped .map with 1/2 instead of letters
6.9 MB
Programs that cannot read letters


--recode A
.raw
3.5 MB
R, Python, genomic prediction


--recode AD
.raw with extra heterozygote columns
7.1 MB
Models with dominance


--recode transpose
.tped .tfam
7.1 MB
Programs that read one SNP per line


--recode vcf-iid
.vcf
7.1 MB
BEAGLE, bcftools, imputation




5.2.1 --recode: back to text
plink --bfile cattle --cow --recode --out cattle_text
head -2 cattle_text.ped | cut -d" " -f1-12
ANG ANG_001 0 0 2 1 A A A A T T
ANG ANG_002 0 0 1 2 A A A A T T
Six columns about the animal, then two letters per SNP: ANG_001 is A/A at snp00001, A/A at snp00002 and T/T at snp00003. The .map file lists the SNPs in the same order. Use this only when a program needs it: the file is 16 times larger than the .bed.


5.2.2 --recode 12: numbers instead of letters
plink --bfile cattle --cow --recode 12 --out cattle_12
ANG ANG_001 0 0 2 1 2 2 2 2 2 2
Here 1 = A1 and 2 = A2 of the .bim file, not “allele 1 and 2 of the chip”. For snp00001 the .bim says A1 = G, A2 = A, so ANG_001’s A/A became 2 2. Missing is still 0 0. Because A1 is the minor allele in PLINK 1.9, the same letter can be 1 in one file and 2 in another file made from different animals. Add --keep-allele-order if a program needs a stable coding.


5.2.3 --recode A: one number per genotype
plink --bfile cattle --cow --recode A --out cattle_add
head -3 cattle_add.raw | cut -d" " -f1-10
FID IID PAT MAT SEX PHENOTYPE snp00001_G snp00002_C snp00003_A snp00004_T
ANG ANG_001 0 0 2 1 0 0 0 1
ANG ANG_002 0 0 1 2 0 0 0 0
Each column header is the SNP name, an underscore and the allele being counted (A1). ANG_001 has 0 copies of G at snp00001 and 1 copy of T at snp00004. Missing genotypes are NA (12,456 of the 1.7 million cells here). Two cautions: the file holds every genotype as text, so for 50,000 SNPs and thousands of animals it gets large and slow to read in R; and if you combine .raw files made separately, check that the counted allele in the headers is the same, or force it with --recode-allele or --keep-allele-order. Add include-alt to name both alleles in the header (snp00001_G(/A)).


5.2.4 --recode AD: additive plus dominance
plink --bfile cattle --cow --recode AD --out cattle_ad
FID IID ... snp00001_G snp00001_HET snp00002_C snp00002_HET
ANG ANG_001 ...    0          0           0          0
Each SNP now has two columns: the count of A1 (0, 1, 2) and a heterozygote indicator (1 for heterozygotes, 0 for both homozygotes). Use it when you fit a dominance effect yourself; the file is twice the size of --recode A.


5.2.5 --recode transpose: one SNP per line
plink --bfile cattle --cow --recode transpose --out cattle_t
head -1 cattle_t.tped | cut -d" " -f1-12
1 snp00001 0.484 484050 A A A A A A A A
Each line is one SNP: the four .map columns, then two letters per animal in the order of the .tfam file (which is a copy of the .fam). Some older programs, and simple per-SNP scripts, prefer this layout.


5.2.6 --recode vcf-iid: VCF for other programs
plink --bfile cattle --cow --recode vcf-iid --out cattle_vcf
grep -v "^##" cattle_vcf.vcf | head -2 | cut -f1-12
#CHROM  POS     ID        REF  ALT  QUAL  FILTER  INFO  FORMAT  ANG_001  ANG_002  ANG_003
1       484050  snp00001  A    G    .     .       PR    GT      0/0      0/0      0/0
PLINK 1.9 writes A2 as REF and A1 as ALT. Since it does not know the genome’s real reference allele, it marks every line PR (provisional reference). Before imputation or merging with sequence data, set the true REF allele (Chapter 14 shows how). vcf-iid uses only the IID as the sample name; plain vcf would write ANG_ANG_001.
A VCF file has only one name per animal, so when PLINK reads a VCF back it tries to split that name at _ into FID and IID. Our names already contain underscores, which gives:
Error: Multiple instances of '_' in sample ID.
The fix is to say how you want the IDs: --double-id (use the whole name as both FID and IID), --const-fid (FID = 0), or a different --id-delim. A VCF also has no sex or phenotype, so add them back with --update-sex and --pheno.

title: 5  Converting, subsetting and merging data
section: 5.3 Step 3: keep or drop animals and SNPs
text:
5.3 Step 3: keep or drop animals and SNPs
Every subsetting flag either reads a list file or takes a rule. The pattern is always the same: add the flag to a command that writes something, and read the line in the log that says how many animals or SNPs are left. Below, every example was run as
plink --bfile cattle --cow --allow-no-sex <flag> --make-bed --out <new name>
and the result is the line PLINK wrote in the log.

5.3.1 Animals from a list: --keep, --remove, --keep-fam
An animal list has two columns, FID and IID, separated by spaces or tabs, one animal per line. Here we make the list of all N’Dama from the breed file:
awk '$3=="NDA" {print $1, $2}' breed.clst > nda.txt
head -3 nda.txt          # NDA NDA_001 / NDA NDA_002 / NDA NDA_003   (140 lines)
plink --bfile cattle --cow --allow-no-sex --keep nda.txt --make-bed --out nda
--keep: 140 cattle remaining.
Among remaining phenotypes, 16 are cases and 124 are controls.
--remove nda.txt does the opposite (221 cattle remaining). --keep-fam reads a list of FIDs only and keeps whole families: a list of HOL_F01, HOL_F02 and NDA_F01 kept 12 animals (three families of sire, dam and two calves).
Things to check. Both IDs must match exactly, including capital letters, and an animal that is in the list but not in the data is skipped without a warning. A test list of three lines (NDA NDA_001, nda NDA_002 with a lower-case FID, and a made-up NDA NDA_999) gave --keep: 1 cow remaining. and no error. So always compare the number in the log with the number of lines in your list (here 140 and 140). A list with only the IID column does give an error: Line 1 of --keep file has fewer tokens than expected.


5.3.2 Animals by a group label: --filter
plink --bfile cattle --cow --allow-no-sex --filter breed.clst HOL --mfilter 1 --make-bed --out hol
--filter: 141 cattle remaining.
--filter reads a file with FID, IID and one or more value columns, and keeps the animals whose value equals the one you give (HOL). --mfilter 1 says which value column to use: 1 is the first column after FID and IID. Without --mfilter, PLINK uses that first column anyway. This is handy when you keep breed, herd or batch in one table and want to pick one level without making a separate list.


5.3.3 Animals by status: --filter-females, --filter-cases, --filter-founders







Flag
Log line in our data




--filter-females
139 cattle removed due to gender filter (222 left; the 137 males and the 2 unknowns go)


--filter-males
keeps the 137 males


--filter-cases / --filter-controls
217 cattle removed due to case/control status (144 cases left)


--filter-founders / --filter-nonfounders
60 cattle removed due to founder status (301 founders left)



These read the .fam file, so they are only as good as the recorded sexes, phenotypes and parents. Animals with unknown sex are removed by both sex filters.


5.3.4 SNPs from a list: --extract, --exclude
A SNP list has one column: the SNP names exactly as in the .bim.
awk '$1 == 6 {print $2}' cattle.bim > chr6_snps.txt      # 210 SNP names
plink --bfile cattle --cow --allow-no-sex --extract chr6_snps.txt --make-bed --out chr6
--extract: 210 variants remaining.
--exclude chr6_snps.txt left 4,590. Names that are not in the data are ignored without a warning, so compare counts again. With --extract range file.txt the file holds regions instead (chromosome, start, end, name).


5.3.5 SNPs by position: --chr, --from-mb, --to-mb, --snp, --window, --autosome








Extra Commands (added to the template above)
SNPs left
What it selects




--chr 14 --from-mb 23 --to-mb 27
86
Chromosome 14 from 23 to 27 Mb (also --from-kb, --from-bp)


--chr 1-5,X
1,060
A range of chromosomes plus the X


--autosome
4,550
Chromosomes 1 to 29 only (no X, Y, MT)


--snp snp02145 --window 500
14
One SNP and everything within 500 kb on either side


--snps snp00001-snp00010
10
A run of SNPs by name, in file order



Position flags read the chromosome and base-pair columns of the .bim, so they depend on the genome assembly the positions come from.


5.3.6 Random SNPs: --thin, --thin-count
plink --bfile cattle --cow --allow-no-sex --thin 0.25 --seed 7 --make-bed --out thin25
plink --bfile cattle --cow --allow-no-sex --thin-count 1000 --seed 7 --make-bed --out thin1000
--thin: 3598 variants removed (1202 remaining).
--thin-count: 3800 variants removed (1000 remaining).
--thin 0.25 keeps each SNP with probability 0.25, so you get about a quarter (1,202 of 4,800); --thin-count 1000 keeps exactly 1,000. Without --seed, PLINK takes its seed from the computer’s clock and writes it in the log (Random number seed: 1794946461), so two runs a few seconds apart pick different SNPs. Set --seed and the same command always gives the same SNPs. Random thinning ignores LD; for analyses that need roughly independent SNPs, prune instead (Chapter 9).
Two habits worth forming: keep your list files, because they are the exact record of what you did, and read the “remaining” line of the log every time.

title: 5  Converting, subsetting and merging data
section: 5.4 Step 4: merge files from two labs
text:
5.4 Step 4: merge files from two labs
Merging adds new animals as rows and new SNPs as columns. The classic trap is the DNA strand. DNA has two strands that pair A with T and C with G. If one lab reports a SNP as A/G and the other reads the opposite strand, it reports T/C for the same SNP, and PLINK sees four alleles.






Figure 5.1: The merge workflow. The loop through --flip is usually needed once; the checks at the end are always needed.



The whole workflow as commands (each step is explained below):
# 1. try the merge
plink --bfile cattle --cow --allow-no-sex --bmerge batch2 --make-bed --out merged_try1
# 2. it stopped with "3+ alleles": flip the listed SNPs in the second file
plink --bfile batch2 --cow --flip merged_try1-merge.missnp --make-bed --out batch2_flipped
# 3. merge again
plink --bfile cattle --cow --allow-no-sex --bmerge batch2_flipped --make-bed --out merged
# 4. checks: drop strand-ambiguous SNPs, drop SNPs missing in one lab, look for remaining flips
awk '($5=="A"&&$6=="T")||($5=="T"&&$6=="A")||($5=="C"&&$6=="G")||($5=="G"&&$6=="C"){print $2}' merged.bim > ambiguous.txt
plink --bfile merged --cow --allow-no-sex --exclude ambiguous.txt --geno 0.05 --make-bed --out merged_clean
plink --bfile merged_clean --cow --allow-no-sex --flip-scan --out fscan
step 1: Error: 39 variants with 3+ alleles present.
step 2: --flip: 39 SNPs flipped.
step 3: 4920 variants and 401 cattle pass filters and QC.
step 4: 177 ambiguous SNPs; --exclude: 4743 variants remaining.
        816 variants removed due to missing genotype data (--geno).
        3927 variants and 401 cattle pass filters and QC.
        --flip-scan: 10 variants with at least one negative LD match.
The --geno 0.05 in step 4 removed 816 SNPs. That is not a quality problem: those are the SNPs on only one lab’s chip (720 typed only by the first lab and 120 only by the second, minus the few already removed as ambiguous), which are missing for every animal of the other lab. Whether to keep them is a decision: drop them for analyses that need the same SNPs in every animal (PCA, relatedness, GRM), or keep them and impute (Chapter 14).
Our second lab sent 40 animals and 4,200 SNPs, with 40 SNPs on the opposite strand:
plink --bfile cattle --cow --allow-no-sex --bmerge batch2 --make-bed --out merged_try1
40 cattle to be merged from batch2.fam.
Of these, 40 are new, while 0 are present in the base dataset.
4200 markers to be merged from batch2.bim.
Of these, 120 are new, while 4080 are present in the base dataset.
Error: 39 variants with 3+ alleles present.
* If you believe this is due to strand inconsistency, try --flip with
  merged_try1-merge.missnp.
Flip those SNPs in the second file and merge again:
plink --bfile batch2 --cow --flip merged_try1-merge.missnp --make-bed --out batch2_flipped
plink --bfile cattle --cow --allow-no-sex --bmerge batch2_flipped --make-bed --out merged
# 4920 variants and 401 cattle pass filters and QC.
PLINK caught 39 of the 40. The missing one, snp03921, is a C/G SNP: flipping C/G gives G/C, the same two letters, so no error is raised and the alleles are silently swapped. A/T SNPs behave the same way. That is why the safe practice is:

Remove strand-ambiguous SNPs (A/T and C/G) before merging data from different sources. Our file had 143 of them:
awk '($5=="A"&&$6=="T")||($5=="T"&&$6=="A")||($5=="C"&&$6=="G")||($5=="G"&&$6=="C"){print $2}' cattle.bim > ambiguous.txt
Better still, ask both labs to export with the same allele coding (Illumina TOP or Forward strand).
Run --flip-scan, which looks for SNPs whose LD with their neighbours has the wrong sign. It needs strong LD, so on our sparse SNPs it flagged 6 SNPs and missed snp03921. It is useful on dense chips.

Two more things the merge taught us. Without --allow-no-sex, PLINK refused to write the merged file because two animals had unknown sex. And SNPs typed by only one lab are missing for every animal of the other lab, so run --geno (Chapter 6) after every merge.

5.4.1 Comparing the same animals genotyped twice: --merge-mode
When the same animal is in both files, --merge-mode decides what to do with disagreements. Mode 6 does not merge at all; it reports every disagreement. We re-genotyped 10 Angus animals:
plink --bfile cattle --cow --allow-no-sex --bmerge regeno --merge-mode 6 --out mm6
# 48000 overlapping calls, 47754 nonmissing in both filesets.
# 47650 concordant, for a concordance rate of 0.996904.







Mode
What happens to a disagreement




1 (default)
Set to missing


2
Only fill in genotypes missing in the first file


3
Take the second file’s genotype unless it is missing


4 / 5
Never / always overwrite


6 / 7
Report disagreements only (7 ignores those involving a missing call)





5.4.2 Many files at once
printf "part2\npart3\n" > mergelist.txt
plink --bfile part1 --cow --allow-no-sex --merge-list mergelist.txt --make-bed --out rejoined

title: 5  Converting, subsetting and merging data
section: 5.5 Step 5: fix IDs, sexes, SNP names and alleles
text:
5.5 Step 5: fix IDs, sexes, SNP names and alleles
Each update flag reads a small text file and changes the .fam or .bim in the new fileset. The log says how many entries were changed; compare it with the number of lines in your file. Run each update in its own command, because some cannot be combined (--update-parents cannot be used with --update-ids).

5.5.1 Sexes: --update-sex
Chapter 8 shows that ANG_071 and NDA_022 are bulls recorded as cows. The file has three columns: FID, IID and the new sex code (1 male, 2 female, 0 unknown).
printf "ANG ANG_071 1\nNDA NDA_022 1\n" > sex_fix.txt
plink --bfile cattle --cow --update-sex sex_fix.txt --make-bed --out cattle_sexfix
grep -E "ANG_071|NDA_022" cattle.fam cattle_sexfix.fam
--update-sex: 2 cattle updated.
cattle.fam:ANG ANG_071 0 0 2 1
cattle_sexfix.fam:ANG ANG_071 0 0 1 1


5.5.2 Animal IDs: --update-ids
Four columns: old FID, old IID, new FID, new IID. Useful when a lab used its own sample codes and you want herd-book numbers.
printf "ANG ANG_001 ANG BULL_DE_001\n" > new_ids.txt
plink --bfile cattle --cow --update-ids new_ids.txt --make-bed --out cattle_ids
--update-ids: 1 cow updated.
Only the .fam changes; pedigree columns that pointed to the old ID are not updated, so rename parents’ IDs in the children’s lines too (with --update-parents).


5.5.3 Parents: --update-parents
Four columns: FID, IID, sire ID, dam ID. In PLINK a parent must have the same FID as its calf. Chapter 10 finds that the true sire of HOL_F03_C2 is HOL_011, who is in family HOL. If you simply point the calf at HOL_011, PLINK finds no animal of that name in family HOL_F03:
printf "HOL_F03 HOL_F03_C2 HOL_011 HOL_F03_D\n" > new_parents.txt
plink --bfile cattle --cow --update-parents new_parents.txt --make-bed --out try1
plink --bfile try1 --cow --mendel --out try1_mendel
--update-parents: 1 cow updated.
--me/--mendel: 343 Mendel errors detected.      (877 before)
The errors did not fall because the pedigree is now right: they fell because PLINK can no longer find the sire, so it stopped checking that calf at all (877 − 343 = 534, exactly the calf’s errors). The correct fix moves the sire into the family first, then updates the parents:
printf "HOL HOL_011 HOL_F03 HOL_011\n" > move_sire.txt
plink --bfile cattle --cow --update-ids move_sire.txt --make-bed --out fixA
plink --bfile fixA --cow --update-parents new_parents.txt --make-bed --out fixB
plink --bfile fixB --cow --mendel --out fixB_mendel
grep HOL_F03 fixB_mendel.fmendel
--me/--mendel: 346 Mendel errors detected.
  HOL_F03    HOL_F03_S    HOL_F03_D      1    2
  HOL_F03      HOL_011    HOL_F03_D      1    3
Now the calf is checked against its real sire and has only 3 errors, which is normal. Moving HOL_011 into family HOL_F03 also takes him out of family HOL; that only matters for commands that use FID, such as --within without a cluster file.


5.5.4 SNP names and positions: --update-name, --update-map
Two columns each: old name and new name, or SNP name and new base-pair position.
printf "snp00001 BTA1_484050\nsnp00002 BTA1_2223660\n" > new_names.txt
plink --bfile cattle --cow --update-name new_names.txt --make-bed --out cattle_names
printf "snp00001 500000\n" > new_pos.txt
plink --bfile cattle --cow --update-map new_pos.txt --make-bed --out cattle_pos
--update-name: 2 values updated.        1  BTA1_484050  0.484  484050  G  A
--update-map: 1 value updated.          1  snp00001     0.484  500000  G  A
The usual reason is moving a file to a new genome assembly (for cattle, from UMD3.1 to ARS-UCD1.2): you need a table of old name and new position from the chip maker. PLINK does not re-sort the SNPs after --update-map, and SNPs that moved to another chromosome need --update-chr as well. Rewrite the files with --make-bed and check that positions increase along each chromosome.


5.5.5 Which allele is A1: --a1-allele, --keep-allele-order
--a1-allele file 2 1 reads the allele from column 2 and the SNP name from column 1, and makes that allele A1. Here we set A1 to the current A2 for every SNP:
awk '{print $2, $6}' cattle.bim > a2_as_a1.txt
plink --bfile cattle --cow --a1-allele a2_as_a1.txt 2 1 --make-bed --out cattle_swapped
head -1 cattle.bim cattle_swapped.bim
--a1-allele: 4800 assignments made.
cattle.bim:          1  snp00001  0.484  484050  G  A
cattle_swapped.bim:  1  snp00001  0.484  484050  A  G
The genotypes are the same; only the allele being counted changes, so every BETA and log(OR) changes sign and every OR becomes its inverse. The usual reason is to make A1 match a reference (for example the ALT allele of a sequence panel). --keep-allele-order simply stops PLINK from re-choosing A1 as the minor allele in each new file. --indiv-sort f order.txt puts the animals in the order of a file (FID IID per line), which some programs expect.






NotePLINK 2.0



The .pgen format is even smaller (0.35 MB for our data). --recode becomes --export (--export A, --export vcf bgz), --bmerge becomes --pmerge, and --flip stops with an error if a listed variant is not a SNP (an insertion or deletion) unless you add permissive. It flips A/T and C/G SNPs without complaint, exactly like PLINK 1.9, so remove those before merging in either version.
plink2 --bfile cattle --cow --make-pgen --out cattle
plink2 --pfile cattle --cow --export vcf bgz --out cattle

title: 6  Missing genotypes: per SNP and per animal
text:
6.1 Why genotypes go missing
A SNP chip measures two light signals per SNP. When the signals are clear, the calling software assigns AA, AB or BB. When they are weak or fall between the clusters, it gives up and writes 0 0. This happens for two quite different reasons.
So we measure missingness in two directions:
\[
\text{missing rate of an animal} = \frac{\text{SNPs with no genotype in that animal}}{\text{all SNPs}}
\qquad
\text{missing rate of a SNP} = \frac{\text{animals with no genotype at that SNP}}{\text{all animals}}
\]
The call rate is just one minus the missing rate: an animal with 2% missing has a 98% call rate.

6.2 The logic, with a toy example
The two directions are tangled: every missing cell counts against one animal and one SNP. That is why the order of filtering matters. Here is a small table of six animals and eight SNPs. Genotypes are written the way Illumina reports them: AA, AB or BB, with -- for a call that failed.






Figure 6.1: Case 1: one failed SNP. SNP3 could not be read in four animals, so those four look poor. Dropping that SNP first brings three of them back to 0%.



In case 1, the probe for SNP3 failed in four of the six animals (67% missing). That single SNP pushes Animals 1, 3 and 4 to 12% missing and Animal 2 to 25%. If we filtered animals first with, say, a 10% cut-off, we would discard four animals because of one bad probe. Drop SNP3 first and three of them are perfect; Animal 2 keeps one genuine gap (1 of 7 SNPs, 14%).
Now the opposite situation:






Figure 6.2: Case 2: one failed sample. Animal 4’s DNA could not be read at six SNPs, so six SNPs look 17% missing. Dropping the animal first brings every SNP back to 0%.



In case 2, Animal 4’s sample failed at six of eight SNPs (75%). In a table of only six animals, that one sample makes six SNPs look 17% missing. Filter SNPs first and we lose six good SNPs; drop the animal first and every SNP is back to 0%.
The rule behind both cases: a bad SNP inflates every animal’s rate, and a bad animal inflates every SNP’s rate. How much depends on the size of the table. On a chip with 50,000 SNPs, one failed SNP adds only 0.002% to each animal. In a study of a few hundred animals, one failed sample adds a visible amount to every SNP. So in livestock studies, which usually have far more SNPs than animals, bad animals are the bigger threat to SNP call rates.
A practical plan follows from this. First remove only the disasters, with a lenient cut-off in both directions. Then apply the strict cut-offs, animals before SNPs, so that a few bad samples cannot drag good SNPs over the line.






Figure 6.3: A two-round missingness filter, with what each step removed from our data. The lenient round removes only the obvious failures; the strict round handles animals before SNPs.



Each box is one PLINK command, and each command reads the file the previous one wrote:
plink --bfile cattle --cow --geno 0.10 --make-bed --out qc1   # round 1, SNPs
plink --bfile qc1    --cow --mind 0.10 --make-bed --out qc2   # round 1, animals
plink --bfile qc2    --cow --mind 0.03 --make-bed --out qc3   # round 2, animals
plink --bfile qc3    --cow --geno 0.01 --make-bed --out qc4   # round 2, SNPs
Step 3 below shows what each command printed and why the order matters.

7.1 Allele frequency and MAF
At every SNP each animal carries two copies, so 100 animals carry 200 allele copies. The allele frequency is the share of those copies that carry a given allele. The rarer of the two alleles is the minor allele, and its frequency is the minor allele frequency (MAF).
A worked example. Eight animals have these genotypes at one SNP: CT, TT, CC, TT, TT, CT, TT, TT.
So p(C) = 4/16 = 0.25 and p(T) = 12/16 = 0.75. C is the minor allele, and MAF = 0.25. A SNP with MAF = 0 is monomorphic: every animal has the same genotype, so it tells us nothing about differences between animals.

7.1.1 Step 1: compute frequencies
PLINK has four ways to count alleles. All four were run on the same file; here is what each writes and how to read it.
--freq: the minor allele frequency of every SNP
plink --bfile cattle --cow --freq --out freq
head -3 freq.frq
 CHR        SNP   A1   A2          MAF  NCHROBS
   1   snp00001    G    A      0.02492      602
   1   snp00002    C    A      0.04167      600

A1 is the minor allele and MAF its frequency: G is on 2.5% of chromosomes at snp00001.
NCHROBS (chromosomes observed) is 602, not 2 × 361 = 722, because PLINK counts founders only by default (the log says Allele frequencies (founders only)). A calf’s alleles are copies of its parents’ alleles, so counting calves would count some alleles twice. snp00002 has 600 because one founder is missing there.
On the X chromosome a bull carries one copy, so NCHROBS is smaller (497 at snp04551).

Add --nonfounders to count all 361 animals: snp00001 then has MAF 0.0292 from 720 chromosomes. Use the default for QC; --nonfounders is for a population with no pedigree recorded, where every animal is a founder anyway.
--freq counts: the counts behind the frequency
plink --bfile cattle --cow --freq counts --out freqc
head -3 freqc.frq.counts

   1   snp00001    G    A     15    587      0
   1   snp00002    C    A     25    575      1
C1 and C2 are the numbers of A1 and A2 copies (15 / 602 = 0.0249, the MAF above), and G0 the number of founders with a missing genotype. Counts are what you need for minor allele count filters (--mac) and for small samples, where “MAF 0.01” might mean a single copy.
--freqx: genotype counts
plink --bfile cattle --cow --freqx --out freqx

1    snp00002  C   A   1          23      276        0          0          1

--freq --within breed.clst: one line per SNP per group
The cluster file has three columns, FID, IID and group, with no header:

title: 7  Allele frequency and Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
text:
7.2 Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE)
If animals mate at random and nothing else disturbs a SNP, genotype frequencies follow a fixed rule from the allele frequencies p and q = 1 - p:
\[
P(AA) = p^2, \qquad P(AG) = 2pq, \qquad P(GG) = q^2
\]
Take a SNP where p(A) = 0.3 and q(G) = 0.7. The expected shares are 0.3² = 0.09, 2 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.42 and 0.7² = 0.49, so in 100 animals we expect 9 AA, 42 AG and 49 GG.






Figure 7.2: A SNP with too few heterozygotes. Observed counts (orange) differ strongly from Hardy-Weinberg expectations (grey).



The observed counts in the figure (20, 20, 60) give exactly the same allele frequency (A = (2 × 20 + 20) / 200 = 0.3), but only half the expected heterozygotes and more than twice the expected AA animals. A classic cause is a genotype-calling error in which the calling software misses heterozygotes. PLINK tests the departure with an exact test, which works well even for rare SNPs. A small p-value means the genotype counts are unlikely under HWE.
But genotyping errors are not the only cause of departure from HWE. Selection, inbreeding, a deletion on the SNP, and above all mixing populations also do it. That last one is the important trap in livestock.

7.2.1 Step 3: run the test
plink --bfile cattle --cow --hardy --out hwe
 CHR        SNP     TEST   A1   A2                 GENO   O(HET)   E(HET)            P
   1   snp00001      ALL    G    A             0/15/286  0.04983  0.04859            1
   1   snp00001      AFF    G    A              0/3/116  0.02521  0.02489            1
   1   snp00001    UNAFF    G    A             0/12/168  0.06667  0.06444            1
Each SNP gets three lines: all animals (ALL), cases (AFF) and controls (UNAFF). GENO is the count of hom A1 / het / hom A2; O(HET) and E(HET) are observed and expected heterozygosity. Why three lines? A SNP that really causes a disease can be out of HWE in cases for a genuine biological reason. That is why the --hwe filter in PLINK 1.9 uses controls only when a case/control phenotype is present.


7.2.2 Step 4: watch out for the Wahlund effect
When you pool breeds that have different allele frequencies, you always see fewer heterozygotes than expected, even if each breed is perfectly in HWE. This is called the Wahlund effect. Picture one breed where nearly all animals are AA and another where nearly all are GG. Pool them and the “population” has an allele frequency near 0.5, so HWE expects about half the animals to be AG, but almost none are.






Figure 7.3: The same SNPs tested two ways. Pooling three breeds makes 114 SNPs fail at p < 1e-6 (left); testing within each breed makes only the 12 planted errors fail (right).

Pooled at 10⁻⁶, the filter would have thrown away 102 perfectly good SNPs. Within breed, it found exactly the 12 bad ones. So in multi-breed data, run the test in each breed and remove a SNP if it fails in any of them:
for b in ANG HOL NDA; do
  awk -v b=$b '$3==b {print $1, $2}' breed.clst > keep_$b.txt

7.2.3 Step 5: choose a threshold
The p-value threshold works in the opposite direction from MAF: a smaller number is gentler. --hwe 0.001 removes more SNPs than --hwe 1e-10. In livestock association studies, 10⁻⁶ applied within breed is a common choice. For selection-signature work be careful, because strong selection can itself push a SNP out of HWE, and that is exactly what you are looking for.
The options change which animals are tested and how the p-value is computed. On the raw file:
plink --bfile cattle --cow --hwe 1e-6 --make-bed --out h1                     # controls (and founders) only
plink --bfile cattle --cow --hwe 1e-6 midp --make-bed --out h2                # mid-p exact test
plink --bfile cattle --cow --hwe 1e-6 include-nonctrl --make-bed --out h3     # cases too
h1: --hwe: 63 variants removed due to Hardy-Weinberg exact test.
h2: --hwe: 66 variants removed due to Hardy-Weinberg exact test.
h3: --hwe: 114 variants removed due to Hardy-Weinberg exact test.

Default: when a case/control phenotype is loaded, PLINK 1.9 tests controls only, so a real disease SNP that is out of HWE in cases is not thrown away. Like --freq, it uses founders only; add --nonfounders to include calves (which breaks the independence the test assumes).
midp: the mid-p version of the exact test gives slightly smaller p-values (snp02321: 3.7 × 10⁻⁶ instead of 4.7 × 10⁻⁶), so it removes a few more SNPs (66 instead of 63). It is a little less conservative and is often recommended; say which one you used. --hardy midp reports mid-p values.
include-nonctrl: tests all founders, cases included. Use it for quantitative traits or when no phenotype is loaded (then it makes no difference).
On the X chromosome, bulls carry one copy, so PLINK leaves them out of the test.







NotePLINK 2.0



plink2 --freq writes .afreq, --geno-counts replaces --freqx, and --hardy writes .hardy (autosomes) and .hardy.x. --maf works as in 1.9, but --hwe does not: PLINK 2.0 has no special handling of cases and controls, so it tests all founders, cases included. On the raw practice file, plink2 --hwe 1e-6 removed 113 SNPs where PLINK 1.9 (controls only) removed 63 (Chapter 17). For a controls-only filter, test the controls in one run and exclude the failures in the next (60 autosomal SNPs here; the other 3 that PLINK 1.9 flagged are on the X, which PLINK 2.0 tests separately and reports in hwe_ctrl.hardy.x):
plink2 --bfile cattle --cow --keep-if "PHENO1 == 1" --hardy --out hwe_ctrl   # 217 controls
awk 'NR > 1 && $NF < 1e-6 {print $2}' hwe_ctrl.hardy > hwe_fail.txt
plink2 --bfile cattle --cow --exclude hwe_fail.txt --make-pgen --out cattle_hwe
--hwe also takes an optional second number k that tightens the threshold as the sample grows (the cut-off becomes p × 10-nk for n animals). PLINK 2.0 prints a warning suggesting it when the number of genotyped animals varies between SNPs; in multi-breed livestock data the within-breed test above matters far more.

text:
8.1 Heterozygosity and inbreeding
Every animal has an expected number of homozygous genotypes, given the allele frequencies in the population. PLINK compares observed and expected homozygosity with the inbreeding coefficient F:
\[
F = \frac{O(\text{HOM}) - E(\text{HOM})}{N - E(\text{HOM})}
\]
where O(HOM) is the observed number of homozygous SNPs, E(HOM) the expected number and N the number of SNPs with a genotype.

Neighbouring SNPs in strong LD carry the same information, so one region would be counted many times. Prune first (Chapter 9 explains how):

ANG_030, F = -0.72: far too heterozygous. This is the planted contaminated sample: wherever the two mixed animals differ, the machine sees both alleles and calls a heterozygote.
NDA_040, F = 0.43: highly inbred. This is the planted inbred animal.
The N’Dama as a group sit to the right (mean F = 0.16 against 0.04 for the other breeds). F is measured against pooled frequencies here, so the most distinct breed looks inbred. Compute F within breed when you want to compare animals fairly.

A common rule is to remove any animal whose F lies over three standard deviations away from the average.
--ibc gives three other estimators of F, computed SNP by SNP from the genotype and the allele frequency, the way the diagonal of the GRM is (Yang and colleagues, 2011):
plink --bfile cattle --cow --autosome --ibc --out ibc
grep -E "IID|ANG_001|ANG_030|NDA_040" ibc.ibc

They agree on the extremes (the contaminated ANG_030 is negative on Fhat2 and Fhat3, the inbred NDA_040 is high), but for ordinary animals they can differ a lot: ANG_001 has 0.31, 0.05 and 0.19. Like --het, all three depend on the allele frequencies, here pooled over three breeds, so compare animals within a breed and say which estimator you report. Chapter 10 adds a measure that needs no allele frequencies, F_ROH, from runs of homozygosity.

section: 8.2 Sex check from the X chromosome
text:
8.2 Sex check from the X chromosome
A bull has one X chromosome, so all his X SNPs look homozygous: F on the X is near 1. A cow has two X chromosomes and is often heterozygous: F near 0. PLINK compares this with the recorded sex.
plink --bfile cattle --cow --check-sex --out sexcheck
--check-sex: 246 Xchr and 0 Ychr variant(s) scanned, 44 problems detected.
      FID          IID       PEDSEX       SNPSEX       STATUS            F
      ANG      ANG_071            2            1      PROBLEM            1
      NDA      NDA_022            2            1      PROBLEM            1
      HOL      HOL_064            0            1      PROBLEM            1
      NDA      NDA_009            0            1      PROBLEM            1
      ANG      ANG_001            2            0      PROBLEM       0.2541






Figure 8.2: F on the X for every animal, by recorded sex. F above 0.8 is called male, below 0.2 female, and anything between is “unknown”.




ANG_071 and NDA_022 are recorded as cows (2) but have F = 1. They are bulls: real sex errors.
HOL_064 and NDA_009 had no recorded sex (0). Genetically they are bulls.
The other 40 “problems” are cows with F between 0.2 and 0.5. They are not errors. As with the Wahlund effect, mixing breeds inflates F. Run --check-sex within each breed and the 44 problems fall to 11, still including the four real ones.


8.2.1 Adjusting the sex check
The default calls an animal female when its X-chromosome F is below 0.2 and male when it is above 0.8. You can move both thresholds, and you can let PLINK write the genetic sex into the .fam. Here is what each option did on our data:
plink --bfile cattle --cow --check-sex 0.3 0.7 --out sex_37        # female if F < 0.3, male if F > 0.7
plink --bfile cattle --cow --check-sex ycount --out sex_y          # also count Y-chromosome calls
plink --bfile cattle --cow --impute-sex --make-bed --out cattle_sexed
sex_37:       --check-sex: 246 Xchr and 0 Ychr variant(s) scanned, 10 problems detected.
sex_y:        Warning: No Y chromosome data for --check-sex ycount.
cattle_sexed: --impute-sex: 246 Xchr and 0 Ychr variant(s) scanned, 321/361 sexes imputed.

Widening the thresholds (0.3 and 0.7) cut the problems from 44 to 10, still including the four real ones. Most of the other “problems” were cows with F between 0.2 and 0.3, which the breed mixture had pushed up. Widening the window is fine when you can see a clear gap in the F histogram; run the check within breed if you cannot.
ycount also uses the number of non-missing Y-chromosome calls, which separates the sexes much better when the chip has Y SNPs. Our simulated chip has none, so PLINK warns and falls back on the X alone. Real cattle chips usually include some Y SNPs; check that they are coded as chromosome Y (31 with --cow) in your .bim.
--impute-sex writes the genetic sex into the new .fam: 141 bulls, 180 cows and 40 animals set to 0 (unknown). Those 40 were cows whose F fell between 0.2 and 0.8. They were correctly recorded as cows before; afterwards PLINK 1.9 ignores their phenotypes in association tests unless you add --allow-no-sex. So never apply --impute-sex blindly: fix the few clear errors with --update-sex (Chapter 5) instead.

A calf gets one allele from its sire and one from its dam. If both parents are AA, the calf must be AA. A calf that is AG breaks Mendel’s law; this is a Mendel error. Many errors in one family point to a wrong parent. Many errors at one SNP point to a bad SNP.

title: 9  Linkage disequilibrium
text:
9.1 Where LD comes from
When a mutation first appears, it sits on one particular chromosome with one particular set of alleles around it. Every copy of the mutation in later generations descends from that first copy, so at first it always comes with the same neighbours. Each generation, recombination swaps pieces between the two chromosomes of a parent. A SNP 10 Mb away is separated from the mutation quickly; a SNP 10 kb away almost never. So LD is strong between nearby SNPs and weak between distant ones.
In livestock, LD extends much further than in humans, because breeds were founded from few animals and a few popular sires have many offspring (a small effective population size). That is why 50,000 SNPs are enough for genomic selection in cattle.

title: 9  Linkage disequilibrium
text: Figure 9.1: A new mutation appears on one chromosome. Over generations, recombination cuts the chromosome, but the pieces right next to the mutation are rarely separated from it.

title: 9  Linkage disequilibrium
text:
9.2 Haplotypes
A haplotype is the set of alleles on one chromosome copy. With two SNPs, one with alleles A/C and one with alleles G/T, there are four possible haplotypes: A-G, A-T, C-G and C-T. Each animal carries two haplotypes, one from each parent.
From genotypes alone we often cannot tell which haplotypes an animal has. An animal that is A/C at the first SNP and G/T at the second could carry A-G + C-T, or A-T + C-G. Finding the right pair is called phasing. For two SNPs at a time, PLINK can estimate the four haplotype frequencies in the whole group without knowing every animal’s phase (below). Getting each animal’s two haplotypes along a whole chromosome is a different and much harder job, done by programs such as BEAGLE, SHAPEIT and Eagle (Chapter 14).

title: 9  Linkage disequilibrium
section: 9.3 Measuring LD: D, D′ and r²
text:
9.3 Measuring LD: D, D′ and r²
Write fA for the frequency of allele A at SNP 1, fT for the frequency of allele T at SNP 2, and fAT for the frequency of the A-T haplotype. If the two SNPs were independent, the A-T haplotype frequency would simply be fA × fT. D measures how far reality is from that:
\[
D = f_{AT} - f_A \, f_T
\]
D depends on the allele frequencies, so two scaled versions are used:
\[
r^2 = \frac{D^2}{f_A(1-f_A)\,f_T(1-f_T)}
\qquad\qquad
D' = \frac{D}{D_{\max}}
\]
where Dmax is the largest value D could reach with these allele frequencies. r² is the squared correlation between the alleles; it ranges from 0 (independent) to 1 (one SNP perfectly predicts the other). D′ is 1 when at most three of the four haplotypes exist, even if one of them is rare. For association and genomic prediction, r² is the one to use: it tells you how well one SNP can stand in for another.

9.3.1 A worked example with real output
--ld reports the haplotype frequencies of one pair of SNPs. Only animals that are heterozygous at both SNPs have an unknown phase; everyone else’s haplotypes can be read straight from the genotypes. PLINK estimates the frequencies with the EM algorithm: it splits each double heterozygote between the two possible phases in proportion to the current frequency estimates, re-counts, and repeats until the numbers stop changing.
plink --bfile cattle --cow --ld snp02144 snp02145 --out ld_pair
   R-sq = 0.382072       D' = 0.642212

   Haplotype     Frequency    Expectation under LE
   ---------     ---------    --------------------
          AT      0.323442                0.173290
          CT      0.102233                0.252385
          AG      0.083652                0.233804
          CG      0.490672                0.340520

   In phase alleles are AT/CG
Let us check PLINK’s numbers by hand.

Allele frequencies: fA = AT + AG = 0.323 + 0.084 = 0.407, and fT = AT + CT = 0.323 + 0.102 = 0.426.
If independent, AT would be 0.407 × 0.426 = 0.173. That is PLINK’s column “Expectation under LE”: the haplotype frequency expected under linkage equilibrium, the situation in which the alleles at the two SNPs are combined at random.
D = 0.323 − 0.173 = 0.150.
r² = 0.150² / (0.407 × 0.593 × 0.426 × 0.574) = 0.0225 / 0.0590 = 0.382, as PLINK reported.
Dmax = min(0.407 × 0.574, 0.593 × 0.426) = 0.234, so D′ = 0.150 / 0.234 = 0.642, as PLINK reported.

“In phase alleles are AT/CG” means A tends to travel with T, and C with G.






WarningLE is not HWE



The two “equilibria” are easy to mix up. Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (Chapter 7) is about one SNP: are the two alleles inside an animal combined at random, giving p², 2pq and q²? Linkage equilibrium is about two SNPs: are the alleles at SNP 1 combined at random with the alleles at SNP 2 on the same chromosome copy, giving fAfT for haplotype A-T? A SNP pair can be in perfect HWE at both SNPs and still be in strong linkage disequilibrium. The expected values in the table come from multiplying allele frequencies, not from p², 2pq and q².








TipWhy r² can never reach 1 for some pairs



r² can only be 1 when the two SNPs have the same MAF. A SNP with MAF 0.05 and one with MAF 0.40 can never be perfectly correlated, however close they are. This is one reason rare variants are hard to tag with common chip SNPs.

title: 9  Linkage disequilibrium
text:
9.5 Why LD matters in practice
1. Tagging. A chip SNP does not need to be the causal mutation. If it is in strong LD with the causal variant, it shows the association for it. This is how genome-wide association works.
2. The top SNP is not necessarily causal. In Chapter 13 the weaning-weight signal appears at five SNPs in the PLAG1 region, because they are all in LD with each other. Separating the real cause from its neighbours is called fine-mapping. Conditional analysis (--condition, Chapter 13) is the PLINK tool for a first look.
3. Many analyses need independent SNPs. PCA, relatedness, F and admixture assume each SNP is a separate piece of evidence. In a block of ten SNPs in perfect LD, the region would count ten times. So we prune:
plink --bfile cattle --cow --autosome --indep-pairwise 50 5 0.2 --out prune
Pruned 82 variants from chromosome 14, leaving 148.
Pruning complete.  969 of 4550 variants removed.
--indep-pairwise 50 5 0.2 looks at a window of 50 SNPs, removes one SNP from every pair with r² above 0.2, then slides the window 5 SNPs along and repeats. It writes prune.prune.in (SNPs to keep) and prune.prune.out; use them with --extract prune.prune.in. The heaviest pruning happened in the dense regions on chromosomes 14, 6 and 5, as expected. Chapter 17 shows how the three numbers change the result.
4. Summarizing association results. --clump groups significant SNPs that are in LD with each other into one “clump” per signal, so that a list of 50 significant SNPs becomes, for example, 3 independent loci.






NotePLINK 2.0



plink2 --r2-unphased replaces plink --r2, and plink2 --r2-phased replaces plink --r2 dprime (see the box above). --ld, --indep-pairwise, --blocks and --clump work as in 1.9.

text:
10.1 IBS and IBD: two kinds of sharing
At any SNP, two animals can share 0, 1 or 2 alleles. There are two reasons they might share one.
IBD implies IBS, but not the other way round. Two unrelated Holsteins share many alleles by state simply because the alleles are common in Holsteins. Relatedness is about IBD.

Identical by state (IBS): the alleles are the same letter. That can happen by chance, especially for a common allele.
Identical by descent (IBD): the alleles are the same physical copy, inherited from a recent common ancestor.

text:
10.4 Step 2: the genomic relationship matrix (GRM)
A second way to measure relatedness treats each SNP as a small piece of evidence and averages over all SNPs. Write gil for the number of copies (0, 1 or 2) of allele 1 that animal i carries at SNP l, and fl for the frequency of that allele. The genomic relationship between animals i and j is
\[
\hat r_{ij} = \frac{1}{p}\sum_{l=1}^{p}\frac{(g_{il}-2f_l)(g_{jl}-2f_l)}{2f_l(1-f_l)}
\]
In words: standardize each genotype by subtracting its expected value and dividing by its standard deviation, then average the products over all p SNPs. Two animals that carry the same unusual alleles get a positive value; unrelated animals average about zero (and can be slightly negative). This is the GRM of Yang and colleagues (2011), used by GCTA and in GBLUP genomic prediction; VanRaden’s (2008) G matrix is a close relative.

section: 10.5 Step 3: KING, a method robust to structure
text:
10.5 Step 3: KING, a method robust to structure
KING (Manichaikul and colleagues, 2010) estimates kinship without using population allele frequencies. For a pair of animals i and j it counts three things at the SNPs where both are genotyped: the SNPs where both are heterozygous (NAa,Aa), the SNPs where they are opposite homozygotes, AA against aa (NAA,aa), and each animal’s own number of heterozygous SNPs (NAa(i) and NAa(j)). Opposite homozygotes are impossible for a parent and its calf, and rare for close relatives, so they count against relatedness; shared heterozygotes count for it.
The simplest form, for animals from one homogeneous population, is
\[
\hat\phi_{ij} = \frac{N_{Aa,Aa} - 2\,N_{AA,aa}}{N_{Aa}^{(i)} + N_{Aa}^{(j)}}
\]
PLINK 2.0 uses the version Manichaikul and colleagues recommend when the two animals may come from different populations (their “between-family” estimator), which divides by the heterozygote count of the less heterozygous animal, written here as i:
\[
\hat\phi_{ij} = \frac{N_{Aa,Aa} - 2\,N_{AA,aa}}{2\,N_{Aa}^{(i)}} + \frac{1}{2} - \frac{N_{Aa}^{(i)} + N_{Aa}^{(j)}}{4\,N_{Aa}^{(i)}}
\]
A check with real numbers, for the sire HOL_F01_S and his calf HOL_F01_C1 (autosomes, 4,495 SNPs typed in both): NAa,Aa = 608, NAA,aa = 2, and the two animals have 1,272 and 1,291 heterozygous SNPs. The second formula gives (608 − 4)/(2 × 1,272) + 0.5 − 2,563/(4 × 1,272) = 0.2337, exactly PLINK’s KINSHIP of 0.233687 (the first gives 0.236). The expected value for parent and offspring is 0.25. title: 10  Relatedness, inbreeding and runs of homozygosity
text:
10.6 Step 4: runs of homozygosity (ROH)
An inbred animal inherited the same long stretch of chromosome from both parents, because both got it from a common ancestor. That stretch shows up as a long run of homozygous SNPs, a run of homozygosity (ROH). The share of the genome covered by ROH is F_ROH, a genomic inbreeding coefficient widely used in livestock:
\[
F_{ROH} = \frac{\text{total length of ROH in the animal}}{\text{length of the genome covered by SNPs}}
\]
Long ROH come from recent inbreeding (the common ancestor was a few generations back); short ROH from old inbreeding. A common rule of thumb is that an ROH of length L cM traces back to a common ancestor about 50/L generations ago.
plink --bfile cattle --cow --autosome --homozyg --homozyg-density 1000 --homozyg-gap 3000 \
      --homozyg-snp 30 --homozyg-kb 10000 --homozyg-window-snp 30 --out roh

title: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis
text:
11.1 The idea in two SNPs
Imagine only two SNPs, and plot every animal by its (standardised) genotype at SNP A and SNP B. If the two SNPs are correlated, the cloud of points is stretched along a diagonal.
PCA finds new axes for the same cloud:
Each PC is described by two things:
In the toy example, PC1 has eigenvalue 2.09 and PC2 only 0.14: PC1 carries 94% of the variation, so one number per animal describes almost everything the two SNPs say. With real data we do the same thing with thousands of SNPs at once.
crumbs: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis

title: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis
text:
Figure 11.1: Left: animals plotted by two correlated SNPs. The red arrow (PC1) points along the direction where the animals differ most; the blue arrow (PC2) is at right angles to it. Right: the same animals after rotating the axes onto the PCs.





The first principal component (PC1) is the direction along which the animals differ the most.
PC2 is the direction of most remaining variation, at right angles to PC1, and so on.



An eigenvector: the direction itself, a list of weights, one per SNP (PLINK calls these the SNP loadings or variant weights). Projecting an animal onto that direction gives its PC score: the number you plot.
An eigenvalue: how much of the variation lies along that direction. A big eigenvalue means a PC that separates animals strongly.
crumbs: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis

title: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis
text:
11.2 How PLINK computes it
PLINK first builds the genomic relationship matrix (GRM) from Chapter 10: one row and one column per animal, filled with the standardised genotype products averaged over SNPs. Then it finds the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of that matrix. Each eigenvector of the GRM has one value per animal: those values are the PC scores. In matrix language, if G is the GRM,
\[
\mathbf{G}\,\mathbf{v}_k = \lambda_k\,\mathbf{v}_k
\]
where vk is the k-th eigenvector (the scores of all animals on PC k) and λk its eigenvalue. The eigenvalues add up to the total variation, which equals the sum of the diagonal of G (its trace, roughly the number of animals). So the share of variation explained by PC k is
\[
\text{\% variance of PC}_k = \frac{\lambda_k}{\text{trace}(\mathbf{G})} \times 100
\]






WarningThe most common PCA mistake



PLINK only writes the top 20 eigenvalues (or as many as you ask for). Many tutorials divide each eigenvalue by the sum of those values. That gives the share among the first few PCs, not of the total, and it exaggerates badly. In our data PC1 is 45% of the first ten eigenvalues but only 8.6% of the total variation. To get the true total, run --make-rel on the same SNPs and add up the diagonal (in R: sum(diag(G))), or use the number of animals as an approximation.

title: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis
text:
11.3 Step 1: prepare the data
PCA is sensitive to things that are not population structure. Before running it:

Filter rare SNPs (--maf 0.05). PLINK 1.9 returned all-zero PCs with monomorphic SNPs present, and PLINK 2.0 refuses to run.
Prune for LD (--indep-pairwise 50 5 0.2), so that a block of correlated SNPs does not dominate a PC.
Use autosomes only (PLINK does this for you).
Remove duplicates, and ideally close relatives. A family or a duplicate pair can take over a whole PC (Step 6).

plink --bfile cattle --cow --maf 0.05 --autosome --indep-pairwise 50 5 0.2 --out prune
plink --bfile cattle --cow --extract prune.prune.in --pca 10 header tabs var-wts --out pca

11.5 Step 3: how many PCs matter? The scree plot






Figure 11.2: Scree plot. Bars show the share of the total variation (eigenvalue divided by 384.5, the trace of the GRM); numbers on the bars are the raw eigenvalues.



The first two eigenvalues (32.9 and 19.1) stand far above the rest, which flatten out near 2.5 to 2.9. That “elbow” after PC2 tells us there are two strong axes of structure: with three breeds, you need two axes to separate them (in general, k groups need k - 1 PCs). After the elbow, PCs mostly describe noise or small family groups. For association studies, people usually include the PCs up to the elbow, and often a few more for safety (Chapter 12 uses PC1 and PC2).

title: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis
text:
11.6 Step 4: plot the animals






Figure 11.3: PC1 against PC2 and PC1 against PC3, coloured by recorded breed. Axis labels give the share of the total variation.




PC1 (8.6%) separates N’Dama from the two European breeds. PC2 (5.0%) separates Angus from Holstein. That matches what we know about cattle history: the African taurine N’Dama is the most distinct.
ANG_066, recorded as Angus, sits inside the Holstein cloud. It is a mislabelled Holstein.
HOL_077, recorded as Holstein, sits halfway between Holstein and N’Dama. It is a crossbred: a 50:50 cross falls in the middle of the line between its two parent breeds.

title: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis
section: 11.8 Step 6: watch out for families and duplicates
text:
11.8 Step 6: watch out for families and duplicates
A group of close relatives can take over a PC of its own, a problem described in many GWAS teaching notes (see Appendix C). It happened to our PC3: the animals with extreme PC3 scores were all members of a few Holstein families (F01, F14, F07, F11), because a sire, a dam and two calves share a lot of genome. PC3 described families, not breeds.
The fix is to compute the PCs on unrelated animals only and then project everyone else onto those PCs, using the SNP loadings. PLINK 2.0 does both steps:
# 1. PCs from the 301 founders only, saving the SNP loadings
plink2 --bfile cattle --cow --extract prune.prune.in --keep founders.txt \
       --maf 0.05 --freq --pca 10 allele-wts --out pcaF
# 2. project all 361 animals onto those PCs
plink2 --bfile cattle --cow --extract prune.prune.in --read-freq pcaF.afreq \
       --score pcaF.eigenvec.allele 2 6 header-read no-mean-imputation variance-standardize \
       --score-col-nums 7-16 --out proj






Figure 11.4: Left: PCs computed on all animals; family members (orange) stretch PC3. Right: PCs computed on founders only, with everyone projected. The families now sit inside their breed.



In the right panel the families sit neatly inside their breed. But two animals now stand far out on PC3: HOL_050 and HOL_050_rep, the duplicate sample from Chapter 10. Two identical “founders” are the most extreme family possible. So the rule is: remove duplicates and relatives first, then compute PCs, then project.
crumbs: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis

title: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis
text:
11.9 Step 7: check the SNP loadings
The loadings tell you which SNPs build each PC. For population structure they should be spread along the whole genome. A single tall peak means one region (often a large inversion or a region under strong selection) is driving the PC, and your LD pruning was not enough.






Figure 11.5: Absolute PC1 loadings along the genome. They are spread evenly, so PC1 reflects genome-wide breed differences.

title: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis
section: 11.10 PCA and MDS: two roads to the same map
text:
11.10 PCA and MDS: two roads to the same map
An older alternative to PCA is multidimensional scaling (MDS) of the pairwise distances between animals. PLINK can do it directly:
plink --bfile cattle --cow --extract prune.prune.in --cluster --mds-plot 4 --out mds
# or: MDS in R from a PLINK distance matrix
d   <- as.matrix(read.table("dist.mdist"))          # plink ... --distance-matrix --out dist
ids <- read.table("dist.mdist.id")
mds <- cmdscale(d, k = 5, eig = TRUE)
pct <- round(mds$eig / sum(mds$eig) * 100, 2)      # here all eigenvalues are available
MDS works on IBS distances and PCA on the GRM. In our data both gave the same picture: three tight clouds, ANG_066 with the Holsteins and HOL_077 in the middle. PCA is faster for big data and is the standard choice for covariates, and the PLINK 2.0 --pca approx option handles tens of thousands of animals.

11.11 Using clustering to name the groups
PCA shows structure; clustering assigns animals to groups. --cluster --K 3 split our animals into 79 Angus; 141 Holsteins plus ANG_066; and 140 N’Dama, with HOL_077 in the Holstein cluster. Chapter 17 shows how --ppc and --mc change the clusters. For admixture proportions (for example, what share of HOL_077 is N’Dama), use ADMIXTURE on the pruned PLINK files.

12.1 Step 1: the allelic test
From here on we use the cleaned file cattle_qc (351 animals, 4,443 SNPs; Chapter 19 lists the QC steps). The disease is BRD: 138 cases and 213 controls. Every command starts with plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex.
Count alleles in cases and controls and put them in a 2 × 2 table. For our true BRD SNP:
The A allele makes up 62% of case chromosomes but only 40% of control chromosomes. The chi-square test (1 degree of freedom) asks whether a difference that large could easily happen by chance. The odds ratio summarises the size of the effect:
\[
OR = \frac{171/105}{168/254} = 2.46
\]
The odds of carrying A are 2.46 times higher on a case chromosome than on a control chromosome.
Something is very wrong: hundreds of SNPs have p-values below 10⁻¹⁰, and the true BRD SNP is only 238th.
