section: 12.2 Step 2: spot stratification with λ, the Manhattan plot and the QQ plot
text:
12.2 Step 2: spot stratification with λ, the Manhattan plot and the QQ plot
BRD is far more common in Holsteins (84 of 141) than in N’Dama (6 of 80). Any SNP whose frequency differs between those breeds therefore looks associated with BRD. This is population stratification, the most common cause of false positives in livestock studies.
The genomic inflation factor λ measures it. If almost no SNP is truly associated, the median chi-square across the genome should be 0.455 (the median of a chi-square with 1 degree of freedom):
\[
\lambda = \frac{\text{median}(\chi^2_{\text{observed}})}{0.455}
\]
λ near 1.0 is healthy, above 1.05 to 1.1 deserves attention, and 10.2 is a disaster.






Figure 12.1: Manhattan plots for BRD. Each dot is a SNP; height is -log10(p); the dashed line is the Bonferroni threshold. Top: naive test. Bottom: logistic regression with PC1 and PC2 as covariates.









Figure 12.2: QQ plot: observed against expected -log10(p). Under no association the points follow the line. The naive test (orange) climbs off the line from the start, the sign of inflation; the corrected test (blue) follows the line until the one true signal.

Bonferroni, Holm and Šidák control the chance of even one false positive and are strict; FDR_BH controls the expected share of false positives among the hits and is gentler, which suits screening many SNPs. GC divides each chi-square by λ, so it only makes sense when λ is close to 1 and the inflation is spread evenly. Note that these corrections treat the SNPs as independent; with SNPs in LD they are conservative, which is why permutation (Chapter 13) gives a sharper genome-wide threshold.

12.4 Step 4: other tests for the same question

12.4.1 Fisher’s exact test
The chi-square test is an approximation that becomes unreliable when a table cell has fewer than about 5 counts (rare SNPs, small studies). Fisher’s exact test computes the exact probability:
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --assoc fisher --out a_fisher
For snp00706 it gave p = 1.36 × 10⁻⁸, close to the chi-square’s 1.04 × 10⁻⁸, because the counts are large.


12.4.2 Genotype models: trend, dominant, recessive and general
The allelic test counts alleles. --model counts animals by genotype and asks several questions at once:

TREND and ALLELIC are strongest, which fits an additive effect (each copy of A adds the same amount of risk), and that is how the SNP was simulated. GENO, DOM and REC are only computed when every cell has at least 5 animals; --cell 0 removes that rule.


12.4.3 Model comparison: is the effect additive?
--logistic --genotypic fits two terms per SNP: ADD (0, 1 or 2 copies of A1) and DOMDEV (1 for heterozygotes, 0 otherwise). DOMDEV measures how far the heterozygote is from halfway between the two homozygotes.
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --logistic --covar pcs.txt --genotypic --out lg_geno
   5   snp00706   62019439    A        ADD      349      3.325        5.573    2.505e-08
   5   snp00706   62019439    A     DOMDEV      349      1.026      0.09652       0.9231
   5   snp00706   62019439    A   GENO_2DF      349         NA        31.19    1.688e-07
DOMDEV p = 0.92: no sign of dominance, so the simpler additive model is right. The fitted dominant and recessive models were weaker (p = 7.5 × 10⁻⁶ and 3.3 × 10⁻⁶).






WarningOR = inf



One SNP in this run reported OR = inf with p = 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁰³. An infinite odds ratio means one genotype appears only in cases or only in controls (“complete separation”), and the regression breaks. Always look at the genotype counts (--model) before believing such a result.




12.4.4 Stratified tests: Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel and Breslow-Day
Instead of a regression, you can split animals into strata (breeds) and combine the 2 × 2 tables:
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --mh --within breed.clst --out mh
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --bd --within breed.clst --out bd
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --homog --within breed.clst --out homog

12.5 Which test should I use?






Figure 12.3: A simple guide to choosing a case/control test, with the PLINK command for each box.



Each box of the figure as a command on the cleaned data, with the result for the BRD SNP snp00706 from the sections above:
# one breed, rare SNPs or a small study: exact test
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --assoc fisher --out a_fisher          # p = 1.4e-08
# one breed, common SNPs: allelic and genotype tests, and check lambda
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --model --out m_all                    # TREND p = 9.8e-09
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --assoc --adjust --out a_basic         # lambda = 10.19 here!
# several breeds: model the structure
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --logistic --covar pcs.txt --hide-covar --adjust --out lg_pc   # p = 2.3e-08, lambda 1.04
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --mh --within breed.clst --out mh                              # p = 9.9e-09
# then: same effect in every breed? additive?
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --bd --within breed.clst --out bd                              # Breslow-Day p = 0.59
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --logistic --covar pcs.txt --genotypic --out lg_geno          # DOMDEV p = 0.92
Our data have three breeds, so the right-hand branch applies; the λ of 10.19 from the plain --assoc is the warning sign that sends you there.






NotePLINK 2.0

plink2 --bfile cattle_qc --cow --glm hide-covar firth-fallback --covar pcs.txt --adjust --out glm_brd
It gave the same answer: snp00706, OR 3.319, p = 2.29 × 10⁻⁸, λ = 1.04.

title: 13  Families, quantitative traits, interaction and permutation
text:
13.1 Quantitative traits
For a trait like weaning weight (WWT), PLINK fits a straight line: weight against the number of copies of allele A1 (0, 1 or 2). The slope, BETA, is the average change in kilograms per copy.
\[
\text{WWT} = \mu + \beta \times (\text{copies of A1}) + \text{covariates} + \text{error}
\]
You do not pick “case/control” or “quantitative” yourself: PLINK looks at the phenotype. If it only contains 1, 2 and missing, it is case/control; otherwise it is quantitative. The same --assoc flag then writes .assoc or .qassoc.

Case/control coded 0/1. PLINK 1.9 expects 1 = control and 2 = case, with 0 and -9 meaning missing. We recoded BRD as 0 (healthy) and 1 (sick) and ran the same test:

13.2 SNP-by-environment interaction
Does a SNP’s effect depend on the environment? In the simulation, snp01540 adds weight only in the feedlot.






Figure 13.3: Weaning weight (as deviation from breed mean) by genotype at snp01540, on pasture and in the feedlot. The lines are parallel if there is no interaction; here only the feedlot line slopes.



--interaction adds a SNP × covariate term for every covariate, and --parameters keeps only the terms you want. The numbering is: 1 = ADD, then the covariates in file order (2 to 6), then ADD × each covariate in the same order (7 to 11). So ADD × FEEDLOT is 10.
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --pheno pheno.txt --pheno-name WWT \
      --linear --covar cov_all.txt --interaction --parameters 1-6,10 --out lin_int
  10   snp01540   52104483    T         ADD      347    -0.3653      -0.2039       0.8385
  10   snp01540   52104483    T     FEEDLOT      347      23.19        7.813    7.086e-14
  10   snp01540   52104483    T ADDxFEEDLOT      347     -10.51       -4.051    6.322e-05
On pasture (FEEDLOT = 0), the T allele does nothing (BETA -0.37, p = 0.84). In the feedlot, each T allele costs an extra 10.5 kg (p = 6.3 × 10⁻⁵; 12 kg was planted).
PLINK 1.9 also has --gxe, which fits the SNP separately in two groups and compares the slopes:
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --pheno pheno.txt --pheno-name WWT --gxe --covar env.txt --out gxe
env.txt gives each animal a group (1 or 2). Across all breeds, --gxe gave p = 0.13, because it cannot include other covariates and breed differences blur the slopes. Within Holsteins only, the slopes were 0.34 kg (pasture) and -11.5 kg (feedlot), p = 0.0096. So prefer --linear --interaction with covariates; for case/control traits use --logistic --interaction. Chapter 16 adds continuous environments.

section: 13.4 Relatives and breeds together: mixed models
text:
13.4 Relatives and breeds together: mixed models
Principal components remove the broad structure (breeds), but livestock data also contain many close relatives: half sibs by the same bull, full-sib families, cousins. Relatives share chromosome segments, so their phenotypes are correlated in ways a few PCs cannot capture, and test statistics stay slightly inflated (λ = 1.10 above). The standard answer in livestock genetics, and in most GWAS of related animals, is a linear mixed model:
\[
\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{g}\,\beta + \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{e},
\qquad \mathbf{u} \sim N(\mathbf{0},\, \sigma^2_g\,\mathbf{G}),
\qquad \mathbf{e} \sim N(\mathbf{0},\, \sigma^2_e\,\mathbf{I})
\]
X b holds the fixed covariates (sex, feedlot, age, and PCs if you wish), g β is the SNP being tested, u is each animal’s polygenic (breeding) value, and G is the genomic relationship matrix from Chapter 10. Animals that are closely related according to G are expected to have similar u, so the model accounts for every degree of relatedness at once, from breed to full sib. It is the same model as GBLUP, with one SNP added as a fixed effect.
PLINK does not fit mixed models. It prepares the data, and a dedicated program fits the model. The common choices are GCTA (--mlma, --mlma-loco; Yang and colleagues, 2014), GEMMA (-lmm; Zhou and Stephens, 2012) and, for very large data, BOLT-LMM or REGENIE. These programs read PLINK .bed/.bim/.fam files directly; PLINK 2.0 can also write the GRM in GCTA’s binary format:
plink2 --bfile cattle_qc --cow --autosome --maf 0.05 --make-grm-bin --out grm   # grm.grm.bin, .grm.N.bin, .grm.id
(With --maf 0.01 PLINK 2.0 refused, because it considers a GRM unreliable when the rarest SNP has a frequency below a quarter of 1/√n, here 0.013 for 351 animals.)
The commands for GCTA and GEMMA look like this. They are shown for reference and were not run for this book, because those programs could not be installed in the environment it was built in:
gcta64 --mlma-loco --bfile cattle_qc --autosome-num 29 --pheno wwt.phen \
       --qcovar qcovar.txt --covar covar.txt --out wwt_mlma          # GCTA
gemma -bfile cattle_qc -gk 1 -o grm                                  # GEMMA: 1. relationship matrix
gemma -bfile cattle_qc -k output/grm.cXX.txt -lmm 4 -c covar_gemma.txt -o wwt   # 2. association
To show what a mixed model does to the results, we fitted one with a short Python program written for this book, scripts/lmm_gwas.py. It follows the approach of EMMAX and GCTA’s --mlma-loco: the variance components are estimated once per chromosome by REML, and each SNP is then tested with them held fixed. “LOCO” (leave one chromosome out) means the GRM used when testing a SNP on chromosome 14 is built from the other 28 chromosomes, so the SNP is not fitted twice, once as a fixed effect and once inside G.
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --autosome --recode A --out geno
python3 scripts/lmm_gwas.py geno.raw cattle_qc.bim pheno.txt WWT cov_all.txt SEX_M,FEEDLOT,AGE lmm_noPC.txt

The GRM alone took λ from 21.9 to 1.06: the model learned the breed structure and the families from the genotypes, without being told about either. Its REML estimate of the SNP heritability was 0.58, because it counted the large breed differences as “genetic”. Adding the two PCs as fixed effects took the breed means out of the polygenic part (heritability 0.29) and gave the cleanest test statistics of all (λ = 1.03), with the PLAG1 SNP as strong as before. That combination, PCs or breed as fixed effects plus the GRM as a random effect, is the usual recommendation for multi-breed livestock data. In our small dataset the mixed model did not move the weaker QTL up the list; its benefit is that the p-values you report can be trusted.

13.5 Family-based tests

13.5.1 The transmission disequilibrium test (TDT)
A heterozygous parent (Aa) passes A or a to a calf with a 50:50 chance, whatever its breed. If sick calves received A much more than half the time, A is linked to the disease. Because the comparison is inside the family, breed differences cannot fool it.
\[
\chi^2_{TDT} = \frac{(T - U)^2}{T + U}
\]
where T is the number of times A was transmitted from a heterozygous parent to an affected calf, and U the number of times it was not.
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --tdt --out tdt
 CHR      SNP   A1 A2   T   U   OR   CHISQ      P   A:U_PAR  CHISQ_PAR   P_PAR  CHISQ_COM   P_COM
   5 snp00706    A  C  16   8    2   2.667 0.1025       9:2      3.769  0.0522      6.081 0.01366
The direction is right (OR = 2) but p = 0.10: our 30 families give only 24 informative transmissions. A TDT needs hundreds of trios. Options: --tdt poo splits transmissions by parent of origin (11:5 from sires, 5:3 from dams here), --tdt exact gives exact p-values, --tdt perm empirical ones.

13.6 Asymptotic and empirical p-values
A normal (asymptotic) p-value comes from a formula that assumes a large sample and a well-behaved test. A permutation test makes no such assumption: it shuffles the phenotypes among the animals many times, recomputes the test each time, and asks how often a shuffled result beats the real one.








Option
What it does
Output




--perm
Adaptive: stops early for SNPs that are clearly not significant
EMP1, NP (permutations used)


--mperm 1000
Exactly 1,000 permutations, with genome-wide correction
EMP1, EMP2


--seed 1
Makes the shuffling repeatable





EMP1 is the empirical p-value for that SNP alone.
EMP2 is corrected for testing all SNPs. In each permutation PLINK keeps the largest statistic across the genome (“max(T)”), and EMP2 is how often that maximum beats this SNP’s real statistic. It is like Bonferroni but accounts for LD.
With N permutations, the smallest possible EMP1 is 1/(N + 1): 0.000999 with 1,000 permutations.

plink ... --logistic --covar pcs.txt --hide-covar --mperm 1000 --seed 1 --out lg_mperm
snp00706 got EMP1 = 0.000999 and EMP2 = 0.000999: significant genome-wide. Its LD neighbour snp00708 got EMP2 = 0.13. With adaptive --perm, snp00706 reached EMP1 = 10⁻⁶ after a million permutations while most SNPs stopped early (an average of 191,673 per SNP).

14.1 What PLINK has to guess: phase
We work on one small region around the BRD SNP, cut out with PLINK 1.9:
Genotypes do not tell you which alleles sit together on the same chromosome copy.
An animal that is A/C at one SNP and G/T at the next could carry its alleles in two ways:
Both give exactly the same genotypes (A/C and G/T), so the chip cannot tell them apart. PLINK uses the EM algorithm: it starts from a guess of the haplotype frequencies in the population, works out how likely each phase is for each animal, updates the frequencies, and repeats until nothing changes. Every phase with probability at least 0.01 is kept as a weighted possibility, and haplotypes rarer than 1% are dropped (--mhf 0.01). Calves are phased with the help of their parents.
You tell PLINK which SNPs make up each haplotype:

14.3 Is it one SNP or the whole haplotype? --chap
A haplotype signal raises two questions:

Does one SNP explain all of it?
Does that SNP matter on its own, or only through its neighbors?

--chap answers both by comparing two models. In the alternative model every haplotype has its own effect. In the null model some haplotypes are forced to share one effect. If forcing them together costs little, the simpler explanation is enough.
# 1. is there any haplotype effect at all?

# 2. is anything left once we allow for snp00706?

text:
14.5 Phasing whole chromosomes
So far PLINK has dealt with phase a few SNPs at a time, and only as haplotype frequencies in the group, or as several weighted guesses per animal. Many modern analyses need more: for every animal, the actual sequence of alleles on each of its two chromosome copies, from one end of the chromosome to the other.

14.5.1 Why you would want phased data







Use
Why phase is needed




Imputation (next section)
The program matches each of the animal’s two haplotypes to haplotypes in a reference panel; nearly every imputation program phases the targets first or while it imputes


Haplotype-based selection signatures (EHH, iHS, XP-EHH)
These statistics follow how far a haplotype stays intact around a core SNP


Parent-of-origin effects and imprinting
You need to know which allele came from the sire and which from the dam


Haplotype models in genomic prediction, local ancestry in crossbreds
The units of the model are haplotypes or haplotype blocks, not single SNPs


Phased r², LD-based estimates of effective population size
The formulas assume haplotype frequencies (Chapter 9)



Single-SNP QC, PCA, relatedness and ordinary association tests do not need phase: they work on genotype counts.


14.5.2 The practice data for this part
The cattle file from Chapter 4 has only a few hundred SNPs per chromosome, which is too sparse for imputation. So this part uses a second simulation, made with the coalescent simulator msprime by scripts/simulate_phasing.py (files in data/phasing/). It models 10 Mb of chromosome 14 (20 to 30 Mb) in two breeds, A and B, that separated 60 generations ago and have each had an effective population size of 150 since then. The two breeds end up with an FST of about 0.08, roughly the distance between two European beef breeds.

14.5.3 How a VCF and PLINK 2.0 store phase
In a VCF, a genotype written with a slash, 0/1, is unphased: the animal carries one REF and one ALT allele, in unknown order. A genotype written with a bar, 0|1, is phased: REF is on the first chromosome copy and ALT on the second, and 1|0 is the opposite. Read along a chromosome, the left-hand alleles form one haplotype and the right-hand alleles the other.
PLINK 2.0’s .pgen format keeps this information. PLINK 1.9’s .bed format cannot: it stores only the number of copies of an allele, so phase is lost the moment data pass through a .bed file.
plink2 --vcf ref_A_hd.vcf.gz --chr-set 29 --make-pgen --out refA
plink2 --pfile refA --pgen-info
These files hold only chromosome 14 and no sexes, so --chr-set 29 (29 autosomes) is all PLINK needs; --cow gives the same results.

  No dosages present

The .bed route lost the phase: --pgen-info on a file made from it says “No hardcalls are explicitly phased” and “REF alleles are all provisional” (the PR flag in the VCF). The PLINK 1.9 route did worse: PLINK 1.9 made the minor allele A1 (Chapter 3) and wrote A1 as ALT, so REF and ALT swapped places and every genotype was recoded. The genotypes are still correct, but this file no longer matches the reference panel, and imputation programs will refuse those SNPs or, worse, treat them as different SNPs. We come back to this below.






WarningKeep phased data out of .bed files



Once data are phased, store them as .pgen or as VCF/BCF, never as .bed. If you must use PLINK 1.9 on them, keep the phased VCF as the master copy. --make-pgen erase-phase removes phase deliberately when you need to.


PLINK 2.0 can write phased data in the formats phasing and haplotype programs read:
plink2 --pfile refA --chr-set 29 --export haps ref-first --out refA_haps    # .haps + .sample (SHAPEIT, IMPUTE, selscan)
plink2 --pfile refA --chr-set 29 --export vcf bgz --out refA_phased         # phased VCF, block-gzipped
plink2 --pfile refA --chr-set 29 --export beagle-phased --out refA_bgl      # old BEAGLE 3 format
--export haps stops with Error: '--export haps' must be used with a fully phased dataset. when you give it the unphased .bed version, a useful safety check. Without ref-first, PLINK lists the ALT allele first in each .haps line, so a 0 means ALT; with ref-first, 0 means REF, as in a VCF. Check which convention the next program expects.
--r2-phased (Chapter 9) uses the real phase when it is there. With unphased data it falls back on EM, and for single pairs of SNPs EM works well: over 85,189 pairs of SNPs less than 200 kb apart, the r² from EM differed from the r² computed with the true phase by 0.003 on average (only 376 pairs by more than 0.05). The unphased r² differed from both by 0.017 on average. So pairwise LD does not need phased data. Whole haplotypes do.


14.5.4 Why we do not phase with PLINK
Three reasons, from the simplest to the most important.

PLINK 1.9 and 2.0 have no phasing algorithm. They store, convert, filter and export phased data, but every phased genotype in a .pgen file was phased by another program.
PLINK 1.07 phases only short windows, each on its own. Its EM algorithm must consider every possible haplotype in a window, and the number of possible haplotypes doubles with each extra SNP (2k for k SNPs). So it works in windows of a few SNPs, and it phases each window separately. We ran it on the 100 target animals:
plink --vcf target_fixed.vcf.gz --chr-set 29 --double-id --keep-allele-order --recode --out target
plink107 --noweb --file target --cow --hap-window 6 --hap-phase --out p107
It wrote 289 separate files (p107.phase-WIN1 to p107.phase-WIN289), one per window of 6 SNPs. Within a window it did well: compared with the true haplotypes, it got the phase right in 96.0% of the 17,397 animal-windows that had at least two heterozygous SNPs. But nothing links window 1 to window 2. To build a chromosome-long haplotype you would have to decide 288 times which haplotype of one window continues which haplotype of the next, and PLINK gives no help with that.
It cannot use the information that makes phasing accurate. Good phasing borrows from many other animals at once, models recombination along the chromosome, allows for genotyping errors, can use a phased reference panel and, in livestock, the pedigree. PLINK 1.07 uses only haplotype frequencies inside each window.



14.5.5 How BEAGLE, SHAPEIT and Eagle phase
Nearly all modern programs build on one idea, the copying model of Li and Stephens (2003). An animal’s chromosome is not unique: over short distances it looks like the chromosomes of other animals in the population, because they share ancestors. So the program describes each chromosome copy of the animal as a mosaic of pieces copied from other haplotypes (the reference panel, or the other animals in the study). Moving along the chromosome, the copy usually continues from the same haplotype, and switches to another one only where a recombination happened in their shared history. Switches are more likely over long genetic distances, and a few mismatches are allowed for mutations and genotyping errors. This is a hidden Markov model: the hidden state is “which pair of haplotypes is being copied here”, and the genotypes are the observations.






Figure 14.1: The copying model in action, for one target animal of the practice data. Each colour is one reference haplotype. With a reference of only 10 animals, each chromosome is copied in many short pieces from different haplotypes; with 150 animals, a close relative in the reference carries the same haplotype along all 10 Mb.



The figure comes from scripts/ls_impute.py, a short program written for this book. It fits the Li and Stephens model directly: it tries every pair of reference haplotypes at every chip SNP, so you can read every step. The Viterbi path of the model (the single most likely mosaic) gives the phased genotypes, and the forward-backward probabilities give the imputed dosages. Real programs do the same job thousands of times faster with clever shortcuts:








Program
How it speeds up the copying model
Notes




BEAGLE 5 (Browning and colleagues, 2018, 2021)
Imputes from a small set of “composite” reference haplotypes built for each target animal; phases in two stages (common variants first, then rare ones); works in overlapping windows
Phases and imputes in one run; reads VCF or its fast bref3 reference format


SHAPEIT5 (Hofmeister and colleagues, 2023; earlier SHAPEIT4, Delaneau and colleagues, 2019)
Uses the positional Burrows-Wheeler transform (PBWT) to pick the most similar haplotypes as copying states
Phasing only (phase_common for common variants, phase_rare for rare ones); can use parent-offspring information (--pedigree)


Eagle2 (Loh and colleagues, 2016)
Finds long shared segments quickly, then runs a copying model on the best candidates
Phasing only, with or without a reference; human genetic maps built in, a constant 1 cM per Mb map supplied for other species



For imputation after phasing with SHAPEIT or Eagle, the usual partners are Minimac4 and IMPUTE5.






TipLivestock have one big advantage: relatives



In a breed with a small effective population size, an animal’s chromosome is often shared almost entirely with a sire, a half sib or a cousin in the reference. That is why the 150-animal panel in Figure 14.1 needed a single piece per chromosome. Programs written for livestock exploit this directly. FImpute (Sargolzaei and colleagues, 2014) first uses the pedigree (family imputation) and then searches the population for long shared haplotypes with overlapping sliding windows; it is widely used in cattle breeding programs. SHAPEIT5 can also use parent-offspring information.

title: 14  Haplotypes, phasing and imputation
section: 14.6 Imputation: filling in the SNPs you did not genotype
text:
14.6 Imputation: filling in the SNPs you did not genotype
Suppose your animals were typed on a cheap chip and a group of reference animals on a dense panel or by whole-genome sequencing. The reference animals show which haplotypes go with which alleles at the missing SNPs, so the missing genotypes can be predicted from the chip SNPs around them.






Figure 14.2: The idea of imputation. Each chromosome copy of the study animal is matched to the reference haplotype it shares; the allele that haplotype carries at the missing SNP is the imputed allele.



In commands, the route from a chip file to imputed data in PLINK 2.0 is the one this section follows step by step:
# Step 1: make REF/ALT match the reference panel, and QC
plink2 --vcf lab_vcf.vcf --chr-set 29 --ref-allele force ref_allele_list.txt 2 1 --export vcf bgz --out target_fixed
# Step 2: phase and impute (BEAGLE in practice; the teaching program here)
python3 scripts/ls_impute.py ref_A_hd.vcf.gz target_fixed.vcf.gz chr14.map target_imputed
# Step 3: measure accuracy (here against the truth; in practice by masking)
python3 scripts/eval_imputation.py target_imputed.vcf.gz truth_target_hd.vcf.gz target_chip.vcf.gz
# Step 4: dosages into PLINK 2.0, quality filter, association
plink2 --vcf target_imputed.vcf.gz dosage=DS --chr-set 29 --make-pgen --out imp
plink2 --pfile imp --chr-set 29 --extract-if-info "DR2 >= 0.8" --make-pgen --out imp_dr2
plink2 --pfile imp_dr2 --chr-set 29 --pheno target_pheno.txt --pheno-name WWT --glm allow-no-covars --out imp
Imputation gives a probability for each genotype, not a certainty. The most useful summary is the dosage: the expected number of ALT alleles, a number between 0 and 2 (Chapter 13). A dosage of 1.97 means “almost surely two copies”; a dosage of 1.1 means “probably heterozygous, but not sure”.

14.6.1 Step 1: prepare the two files so they match
Most failed imputations fail here, not in the imputation program. The target and the reference must agree on:

The genome assembly. All positions must come from the same assembly (for cattle today, ARS-UCD1.2 or ARS-UCD2.0). Never mix files from different assemblies; convert positions first.
The SNP names, positions and alleles. BEAGLE requires reference and target markers to match on CHROM, POS, REF and ALT.
The strand and the REF allele. This is where PLINK 1.9 bites. Our chip data had travelled through PLINK 1.9 once (--make-bed, then --recode vcf-iid), as often happens when a lab sends PLINK files:

# what happened to the chip file before it reached us
plink --vcf target_chip.vcf.gz --chr-set 29 --double-id --make-bed --out lab
plink --bfile lab --chr-set 29 --recode vcf-iid --out lab_vcf
# compare REF/ALT of the target with the reference, SNP by SNP
zcat ref_A_hd.vcf.gz | grep -v "^#" | cut -f3,4,5 | sort > ref_alleles.txt
grep -v "^#" lab_vcf.vcf | cut -f3,4,5 | sort > tgt_alleles.txt
join ref_alleles.txt tgt_alleles.txt | \
  awk '{n++; if($2==$4 && $3==$5) same++; else if($2==$5 && $3==$4) swap++; else other++}
       END {print n, "shared:", same, "same,", swap, "swapped,", other+0, "other"}'
294 shared: 224 same, 70 swapped, 0 other
70 of 294 SNPs had REF and ALT swapped, because PLINK 1.9 had made the minor allele A1. Set the REF allele from the reference panel with PLINK 2.0:
zcat ref_A_hd.vcf.gz | grep -v "^#" | awk '{print $3"\t"$4}' > ref_allele_list.txt   # SNP name, REF allele
plink2 --vcf lab_vcf.vcf --chr-set 29 --ref-allele force ref_allele_list.txt 2 1 \
       --export vcf bgz --out target_fixed
--ref-allele: 70 sets of allele codes permuted.
Warning: 1786 variant IDs in --ref-allele file missing from main dataset.
After this, all 294 SNPs matched. (The warning is expected: those are the SNPs that are only in the reference.) With real data, also look for SNPs whose two alleles are different letters in the two files, which means a strand difference, and remove A/T and C/G SNPs if the strand is uncertain (Chapter 5). BEAGLE’s companion tool conform-gt and bcftools +fixref do these checks for VCF files; with --ref-from-fa, PLINK 2.0 can set REF alleles from the genome’s FASTA file instead of from a panel.

Quality control on both files, as in Chapters 6 to 8, using the same thresholds. Our target passed easily (no SNP above 5% missing, worst animal 1.7% missing, no SNP failing HWE at 10⁻⁶).
One chromosome per run, sorted by position, and the genetic map for that chromosome.



14.6.2 Step 2: run the imputation
The commands for the standard programs look like this. They are shown for reference only: these programs could not be installed in the environment where this book was built, so these four commands were not run here. Check each program’s manual for your version.
# BEAGLE 5: phases the target and imputes in one run
java -Xmx8g -jar beagle.jar gt=target_fixed.vcf.gz ref=ref_A_hd.vcf.gz map=chr14.map \
     out=target_imputed gp=true nthreads=4

# SHAPEIT5 to phase (target as indexed BCF), then Minimac4 to impute
phase_common --input target_fixed.bcf --reference ref_A_hd.bcf --map chr14.gmap.gz \
             --region 14 --output target_phased.bcf --thread 4
minimac4 --compress-reference ref_A_hd.bcf > ref_A_hd.msav
minimac4 ref_A_hd.msav target_phased.bcf -o target_imputed.vcf.gz
A few settings matter for livestock. BEAGLE’s default effective population size, ne=100000, suits large human panels; with unphased targets BEAGLE estimates ne and the error rate from the data before phasing, but for a single breed you can also set a small value yourself. SHAPEIT and Eagle need a genetic map in their own formats; without a map for your species, a constant 1 cM per Mb is the usual stand-in (BEAGLE assumes this when map= is left out). PLINK’s .map file, with its centimorgan column, is exactly the format BEAGLE’s map= expects.
What we actually ran is the teaching program, on the same files:
python3 scripts/ls_impute.py ref_A_hd.vcf.gz target_fixed.vcf.gz chr14.map target_imputed
reference: 150 animals (300 haplotypes), 2080 SNPs; target: 100 animals, 294 typed SNPs shared with the reference
wrote target_imputed.vcf.gz: 2080 SNPs (1786 imputed), 100 animals, 147 s
Its output VCF has the same layout as BEAGLE’s: phased genotypes (GT), dosages (DS) and genotype probabilities (GP) for every animal, and in the INFO column the estimated ALT frequency (AF), the quality score DR2 and the flag IMP for SNPs that were imputed rather than typed:

14     20005399 hd00002 T   C   ... AF=0.3550;DR2=1.000;IMP  GT:DS:GP 0|1:1.000:0.000,1.000,0.000
T_001 is heterozygous at both SNPs; the first was on the chip, the second was imputed (IMP). The phase says G (ALT) at the first SNP sits on the same chromosome copy as T (REF) at the second.


14.6.3 Step 3: how good is it?
In a real study you never see the true genotypes of the imputed SNPs. The standard way to measure accuracy is masking: hide some genotypes you do know (for example, a few reference animals treated as targets, or a few chip SNPs), impute them, and compare. Our simulation gives us the answer key directly, so we imputed the 100 targets five times, with different reference panels, and compared every imputed genotype with the truth (scripts/eval_imputation.py):

What the table teaches:

The reference must contain the breed. 150 animals of the other breed did far worse than 10 animals of the right breed. The target’s haplotypes, shaped by 60 generations of drift in its own breed, were mostly missing from the other breed’s panel. Studies in real cattle agree that the target breed must be well represented in the reference, and that adding other breeds to it can raise accuracy further (Bouwman and Veerkamp, 2014; Pausch and colleagues, 2017). Here adding breed B to a 150-animal breed-A panel changed nothing, because breed A alone was already almost perfect.
More reference animals, better accuracy, above all for rare SNPs. Rare alleles sit on few haplotypes, so a small panel often has no copy of the right one.
Concordance flatters. With the 10-animal panel, 95.3% of genotypes were right, but r² was only 0.73 for rare SNPs. For a SNP with MAF 0.02, calling every animal “homozygous common” is already 96% correct and completely useless. Report r² (or the correlation), not concordance.
Switch errors count how often the phase flips between two neighbouring heterozygous SNPs. Phasing accuracy follows imputation accuracy, because both depend on finding the right haplotypes to copy. Across the same 6-SNP windows used for PLINK 1.07 above, the chromosome-wide phase from the 150-animal reference was right in 99.9% of animal-windows, against PLINK 1.07’s 96.0%. (PLINK 1.07 had no reference panel to help it, which is part of the point.)

DR2 and INFO. Every imputation program reports a quality score per SNP, computed from the dosages alone, without the true genotypes: DR2 in BEAGLE, R2 in Minimac, INFO in IMPUTE. They estimate the r² between dosage and true genotype. A cut-off of 0.8 (sometimes 0.3 to 0.5 for association studies that keep more SNPs) is common.






Figure 14.4: DR2 reported by the 10-animal imputation against the true r², for each imputed SNP. Many SNPs above the 0.8 line (dashed) are really much worse.



A quality score is the model’s opinion of itself, and a model that is wrong can be confidently wrong. With the 10-animal reference our DR2 called 72% of imputed SNPs “good”, yet many of them had a true r² well below 0.8, and across SNPs DR2 and true r² correlated only about 0.5. The scores of BEAGLE and Minimac are better calibrated than this simple program’s, but the lesson holds: use DR2 or INFO to remove bad SNPs, and use masking to measure accuracy.


14.6.4 Step 4: bring the imputed data into PLINK 2.0
PLINK 2.0 imports dosages from a VCF when you name the FORMAT field that holds them:
plink2 --vcf target_imputed.vcf.gz dosage=DS --chr-set 29 --make-pgen --out imp
plink2 --pfile imp --pgen-info
  Explicitly phased hardcalls present
  Explicitly phased dosages present
Both the phase and the dosages are kept. Filter on imputation quality with the INFO field, and run the association test on the dosages:
plink2 --pfile imp --chr-set 29 --extract-if-info "DR2 >= 0.8" --make-pgen --out imp_dr2
# 2080 variants in imp.pvar; 30 excluded by --extract-if-info, 2050 remaining.
plink2 --pfile imp_dr2 --chr-set 29 --pheno target_pheno.txt --pheno-name WWT \

PLINK fills a genotype only when the best guess has a probability of at least 0.9 (--proxy-impute-threshold), so it leaves most genotypes empty, and when it calls, it is right only about 90% of the time. It is a historical tool; use the programs above.


14.6.6 Imputation in livestock: practical advice

Use the target breed in the reference, and include the sires of your target animals if you can: close relatives in the reference give the longest, most accurate matches.
Go up in steps. From a low-density chip, impute first to 50K, then to HD, then to sequence. In Holstein cattle, imputing straight from 50K to sequence gave an accuracy of 0.37 to 0.46 per SNP, and going through the HD panel first raised it to 0.65 (van Binsbergen and colleagues, 2014).
Check accuracy by masking, per SNP and per animal. Animals with few relatives in the reference impute worst.
Treat the X chromosome separately: males are haploid outside the pseudoautosomal region. SHAPEIT5 takes a list of haploid samples (--haploids), and FImpute needs a pedigree for the X.
Keep the dosages. In Fleckvieh and Holstein cattle, dosages of imputed sequence variants agreed better with the true genotypes than best-guess calls did, and were better at detecting causal mutations (Pausch and colleagues, 2017). Analyze dosages with plink2 --glm (or a mixed model, Chapter 13) and filter on DR2 or INFO; round to hard calls only when a later program demands it.
Record everything: assembly, reference panel (breeds, size), program and version, settings, and the quality filter.







NotePLINK 2.0



Neither PLINK 1.9 nor 2.0 has the haplotype tests, --chap, proxy association or the 1.07 imputation heuristic. PLINK 1.9 keeps the LD tools that support this work: --ld, --r2, --blocks (haplotype blocks, as in Haploview), --clump and --show-tags. PLINK 2.0 adds what modern pipelines need around phasing and imputation: it stores phased genotypes and dosages in .pgen files, imports them from VCF and BGEN, exports phased data (--export haps, vcf, bgen-1.2), filters on imputation quality (--extract-if-info, --mach-r2-filter) and tests dosages with --glm. The phasing and imputation themselves are done by BEAGLE, SHAPEIT, Eagle, Minimac, IMPUTE or FImpute.

15.6 Step 5: common CNVs together with SNPs
A common CNV (a copy number polymorphism, CNP) can sit on top of a SNP. An animal can then carry, say, one A allele on one chromosome and a deletion on the other, which normal genotype calling reports as “AA”. PLINK 1.07 stores such data as generic variants in a .gvar file with copy numbers for each allele:
ANG ANG_001 ccnv1 A 1 G 0      # one A copy, the other chromosome deleted
ANG ANG_002 ccnv1 A 1 G 1      # normal heterozygote
We simulated a deletion that raises BRD risk sitting on a SNP that does not:

16.2 Epistasis: SNP × SNP interaction
Sometimes two SNPs only matter together. An epistasis test fits, for each pair, a model with both SNPs and their product, and tests the product term.
The BRD simulation included an epistatic pair, but it was built so that nearly every animal carried the risk combination, so it behaved like a single-SNP effect and the pair test failed (p = 0.57). Real epistasis is often just as hard to see. To show what a detectable interaction looks like, we simulated a second disease, PKE, caused only by the combination of snp01294 (chromosome 8) and snp03388 (chromosome 22).






Figure 16.1: Share of PKE cases for each two-SNP genotype. Risk is high in two opposite corners and low in the other two, so each SNP on its own averages out to nothing.

  22   snp03388   ...  CHISQ 2.893    P 0.08894  OR 0.76

text:
16.3 SNP × environment with a continuous environment
Chapter 13 tested a two-level environment (feedlot or pasture). For a continuous one (age at weaning, temperature-humidity index, rainfall) you use the same --interaction, with one trap. Our first try with AGE in days gave NA for every SNP. The interaction column ADD × AGE (values near 0, 205 or 410) is almost a copy of ADD × 205, so it is nearly collinear with ADD, and PLINK’s collinearity check (--vif, default 50) rejects the model.
The fix is to center the environment, which also makes the ADD term easier to read (it becomes the SNP effect at the average age):
# AGE_C = (AGE - 205) / 10
plink ... --linear --covar cov_c.txt --covar-name PC1,PC2,SEX_M,FEEDLOT,AGE_C \
          --interaction --parameters 1-6,11 --out int_agec
  10   snp01540   52104483    T        ADD      347      -5.29       -3.932    0.0001021
  10   snp01540   52104483    T  ADDxAGE_C      347     0.4663       0.4362        0.663
The feedlot SNP’s effect does not change with age (p = 0.66), which is correct: no age interaction was planted. Across the genome, 1 of 4,443 ADD × AGE_C terms had p < 0.001, close to the 4 expected by chance.






WarningThe -9 trap



Our first centered version, AGE − 205, gave the value -9 to calves weaned at 196 days, and PLINK silently treated them as missing (NMISS fell from 347 to 336). Dividing by 10 avoided it. --missing-phenotype changes the missing code.

title: 16  Beyond single SNPs: gene sets, epistasis, environments and meta-analysis
text:
16.4 Meta-analysis: combining several studies
Each breed (or country, or research group) runs its own analysis and shares only the summary results. A meta-analysis combines them, giving more weight to the more precise estimates. The fixed-effect estimate is
\[
\hat\beta_{\text{meta}} = \frac{\sum_i w_i \hat\beta_i}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad w_i = \frac{1}{SE_i^2}
\]
Step 1: one analysis per breed, with the same A1 allele everywhere (--keep-allele-order) and standard errors (--ci 0.95):
for b in ANG HOL NDA; do
  plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --pheno pheno.txt --pheno-name WWT --keep-allele-order \
        --keep k_$b.txt --linear --covar cov_all.txt --covar-name SEX_M,FEEDLOT,AGE --hide-covar --ci 0.95 --out mk_$b
done
Step 2: combine them.

18.3 Step 2: heterozygosity, PCA and ROH in the cattle
plink --bfile cattle_real_qc --cow --indep-pairwise 50 5 0.2 --out c_prune     # 2,984 of 7,211 SNPs kept
plink --bfile cattle_real_qc --cow --extract c_prune.prune.in --het --out c_het

plink --bfile cattle_real_qc --cow --homozyg --homozyg-density 1000 --homozyg-gap 3000 \
      --homozyg-snp 30 --homozyg-kb 2000 --homozyg-window-snp 30 --out c_roh






Figure 18.1: Real cattle. Left: inbreeding coefficient F from --het, with lines at 3 standard deviations from the mean. Middle: PC1 against PC2. Right: genomic inbreeding from runs of homozygosity.



What the three panels say:

Heterozygosity. F averages 0.001 (SD 0.049), as expected when F is measured against the population’s own allele frequencies. Six bulls lie above +3 SD (F = 0.15 to 0.19). None lies below −3 SD, so there is no sign of contaminated samples. High F in a real herd usually means real inbreeding, not a lab error: these bulls should be checked, not removed.
PCA. PC1 and PC2 explain only 1.7% and 1.4% of the variation (eigenvalue divided by the GRM trace, 501.4; Chapter 11). Compare 8.6% in the simulated three-breed data. There are no separate clouds: this is one breed. The fan shape is typical of a population in which some groups of animals are more closely related than others. With no breed structure, the first PCs often pick up families, so in a GWAS of these bulls a mixed model with the GRM (GCTA, or plink2 --glm with PCs plus a relatedness check) would be safer than PCs alone.
ROH. All 500 bulls carry runs of at least 2 Mb, 4,346 runs in total. F_ROH averages 0.079 (maximum 0.258). The SNPs here cover about 1,048 Mb, so F_ROH is the share of that covered length. The three bulls with the most ROH (ID11528, ID11530, ID11593) are also among the six with the highest F, and across all bulls F and total ROH length correlate at 0.83: two different measures tell the same story.

18.5 Step 4: breed differences in the sheep
plink --bfile sheep_qc --sheep --indep-pairwise 50 5 0.2 --out s_prune         # 843 of 4,686 SNPs kept
plink --bfile sheep_qc --sheep --extract s_prune.prune.in --pca 10 header tabs --out s_pca

Figure 18.2: Real sheep: PC1 separates Jacob from Navajo-Churro.



PC1 explains 9.7% of the variation and splits the two breeds cleanly; PC2 (4.8%) and PC3 (4.3%) describe spread within breeds. FST measures how much of the genetic variation lies between the breeds rather than within them:
\[
F_{ST} = \frac{\text{variance of allele frequency between breeds}}{\text{total variance}}
\]
PLINK computes the Weir and Cockerham estimator for every SNP. The log reports a mean FST of 0.142 and a weighted FST of 0.168: about 15% of the variation separates Jacob from Navajo-Churro. For comparison, FST between European cattle breeds is often around 0.05 to 0.15. Single SNPs with very high FST are candidates for selection signatures, which is a whole topic of its own.
ROH tell a breed story too (Figure 10.3): Jacob sheep carry on average 52.9 Mb of ROH on the two chromosomes (F_ROH about 0.18 of the 291 Mb covered), against 27.0 Mb (about 0.09) in Navajo-Churro.

section: 18.7 Ascertainment bias: the chip decides part of the answer
text:
18.7 Ascertainment bias: the chip decides part of the answer
Every SNP chip is a selection. Its makers first found SNPs by sequencing a few animals (the discovery panel), then kept the SNPs that were common in those animals. That choice, called SNP ascertainment, shapes every statistic you compute from the chip. Breeds like the discovery animals look diverse; breeds that were not in the panel carry many chip SNPs that do not vary in them at all, and look less diverse than they are. For cattle this is well documented: the Bovine HapMap study found that African and Indian cattle had higher heterozygosity than European cattle in sequence data, but lower heterozygosity on SNP arrays, whose SNPs had mostly been found in taurine cattle (The Bovine HapMap Consortium, 2009). This matters directly for work on African breeds such as N’Dama, Sanga or zebu.

18.7.1 A simulation where we know the truth
scripts/simulate_ascertainment.py simulates three breeds with msprime: two European-type breeds, EUR1 and EUR2, that split 40 generations ago, and an African-type breed, AFR, with a larger effective population size and therefore more diversity. The signs to look for in your own output:

--freq --within shows many SNPs with frequency 0 or 1 in one breed only. On the EUR1-designed chip, 41% of SNPs did not vary at all in AFR, against 0.6% in EUR1. When one breed has far more monomorphic chip SNPs than the others, suspect that it was missing from the discovery panel.
The ranking of breeds by heterozygosity can turn upside down. The truth is that AFR is the most diverse breed (0.186 against 0.143). On the EUR1 chip, AFR came out the least diverse (0.200 against 0.328 for EUR1). The multi-breed chip put the breeds back in the right order.
The allele frequency spectrum is flat instead of falling. In sequence data most variants are rare (the grey AFR line falls steeply from the left). On the chip, rare variants are almost absent in the discovery breed, because the panel only kept common SNPs. Any statistic that depends on rare variants (Tajima’s D, some selection scans, demographic inference) is distorted.
Absolute values cannot be compared across SNP sets. Every chip gives far higher heterozygosity than sequence (0.33 against 0.14 in EUR1), simply because it selected variable SNPs. Never compare a heterozygosity from a 50K chip with one from sequence, from another chip, or from another study’s SNP set.
FST between the discovery breed and an outside breed is underestimated (0.285 against 0.313), as reported for cattle when SNPs are chosen from some groups only (McTavish and Hillis, 2015). Between two breeds that are both close to the discovery panel, FST was hardly affected.
Runs of homozygosity change with the SNP set. A SNP that does not vary in a breed always looks homozygous, so it helps a run continue. AFR’s FROH was 0.049 on the EUR1 chip but 0.027 on the multi-breed chip, while EUR1’s moved the other way (0.174 against 0.196). Compare FROH only between animals typed on the same chip, and be careful comparing breeds that differ in how well the chip suits them.
PCA is the most robust. The breeds separated in the same way on all three SNP sets, though the split of variance between PC1 and PC2 shifted. Malomane and colleagues (2018) found the same in chickens, comparing arrays with sequence.



18.7.3 Limiting the damage








Strategy
What it does
In our simulation




Know your chip’s discovery panel
Read the chip paper. For the BovineSNP50 chip, SNPs were found mainly in taurine breeds (Matukumalli and colleagues, 2009); African Sanga breeds were not in the discovery process



Use a chip discovered in all the breeds you compare, or sequence
Removes the cause
Correct ranking of breeds, FST 0.321 against 0.313


LD pruning before diversity statistics
Removes the dense clusters of SNPs the panel favoured; the best of several filtering strategies tested by Malomane and colleagues (2018)
Narrowed the gap (AFR 0.291, EUR1 0.323) but did not restore the right order, and lowered FST (0.160 against 0.313), as they also reported


Compare within the same SNP set only
Use chip results for relative comparisons (animals, herds, generations of one breed), not as absolute diversity



Filter monomorphic SNPs per breed before per-breed analyses
--maf within each breed (Chapter 7), so each breed is described by SNPs that vary in it; report how many were removed per breed



Model the ascertainment
Methods that correct the frequency spectrum when the discovery process is known (Nielsen and colleagues, 2004; reviewed by Lachance and Tishkoff, 2013)



Report it
Name the chip, its discovery breeds and your SNP filters, so readers can judge how far the comparison is fair




The short version: a SNP chip is a good tool for questions within the breeds it was designed for, and a biased one for comparing diversity between breeds, especially when some of them, like many African breeds, were not in the discovery panel. LD pruning helps a little; sequence data, or a chip discovered across all the breeds you study, help most.

p = 0.93 naive, 9.7 × 10⁻¹¹ with covariates; 9.6 kg estimated (Chapter 13)


Weaning-weight QTL snp00891 (LCORL region, +5 kg)
--linear
p = 0.0019, rank 18: real but underpowered (Chapter 13)


Feedlot-only effect snp01540 (+12 kg in feedlot)
--linear --interaction
ADD × FEEDLOT = −10.5 kg, p = 6.3 × 10⁻⁵ (Chapter 13)


Epistatic pair for BRD (snp00210 × snp03131)
--epistasis
Not detected (p = 0.57): almost every animal carried the risk combination (Chapter 16)


Deletion hotspot on chr 7 near 40 Mb, and higher CNV burden in cases
CNV --mperm, --cnv-indiv-perm
34 cases against 6 controls, EMP2 = 0.0001; 4.30 against 2.95 CNVs per animal (Chapter 15)



Almost every planted problem was found, and the two that were not (four SNPs with a handful of random errors, and the weak epistatic pair) are the kind real studies also miss. That is the honest lesson of QC: it catches the big problems reliably and the small ones only sometimes, which is why replication matters.

Four differences catch people out:

Allele order. PLINK 1.9 makes A1 the minor allele unless you add --keep-allele-order. PLINK 2.0 keeps the order from the input and calls the alleles REF and ALT. Effect sizes in --glm are for the ALT allele (or the column A1 in the output).

--hwe ignores case/control status in PLINK 2.0, so the same threshold removes more SNPs than in 1.9 when cases are present.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
Term
Meaning




A1 / A2
The two alleles of a SNP in PLINK 1.9 files. Effect sizes (OR, BETA) are always for A1. By default A1 is the minor allele


Allele frequency, MAF
Share of chromosome copies carrying an allele; MAF is the frequency of the rarer one


Call rate / missing rate
Share of genotypes read successfully; call rate = 1 − missing rate


Case / control
Affected (coded 2) / unaffected (coded 1) animal for a yes/no trait


CNV
Copy number variant: a deleted or duplicated stretch of DNA


Covariate
An extra variable in a model (PCs, sex, herd, age) used to remove its influence


D, D′, r²
Measures of linkage disequilibrium between two SNPs (Chapter 9)


Dosage
Expected number of copies of an allele (A1 in PLINK 1.9, usually ALT in a VCF) after imputation, between 0 and 2


DR2, R2, INFO
Imputation quality scores: the estimated r² between dosage and true genotype, from BEAGLE, Minimac and IMPUTE respectively


Eigenvalue
How much variation lies along a principal component


Eigenvector
The direction of a principal component; its values are the PC scores


EMP1 / EMP2
Empirical p-value from permutation / the same, corrected for all tests


Epistasis
Interaction between two or more loci


F (inbreeding)
Excess homozygosity compared with expectation


F_ROH
Share of the genome covered by runs of homozygosity


Founder / nonfounder
Animal with both parents unknown / animal with at least one parent in the data


FST
Share of genetic variation that lies between populations


GRM
Genomic relationship matrix: relationships between animals estimated from SNPs


HWE
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium: genotype shares p², 2pq and q² under random mating


IBS / IBD
Identical by state (same alleles) / identical by descent (same ancestral copy)


Imputation
Predicting genotypes that were not measured, using a reference panel


KING
A relatedness method that does not need population allele frequencies


λ (lambda)
Genomic inflation factor: median test statistic divided by its expected value; close to 1 is good


LD pruning
Removing SNPs so that the remaining ones are not strongly correlated


LE (linkage equilibrium)
Alleles at two SNPs combined at random on chromosomes; the expected haplotype frequency is the product of the allele frequencies


Li and Stephens model
The “copying model” behind most phasing and imputation programs: a chromosome is described as a mosaic of pieces copied from other haplotypes


MDS
Multidimensional scaling of pairwise distances; an alternative to PCA


Mendel error
A calf genotype that is impossible given its parents’ genotypes


Mixed model
Regression with a random polygenic effect whose covariance follows the GRM; corrects for relatives and structure together


OR / BETA
Odds ratio (yes/no trait) / regression slope (measured trait) per copy of A1


PCA
Principal component analysis: a few axes that summarize genetic differences between animals


Phase
Which alleles sit together on the same chromosome copy; 0\|1 in a VCF is phased, 0/1 unphased


PI_HAT
Estimated share of the genome two animals share IBD


Population stratification
False associations caused by differences in both allele frequency and trait between groups


Reference panel
Animals typed at high density (or sequenced) and phased, used to impute others


ROH
Run of homozygosity: a long homozygous stretch inherited from a common ancestor


Strand flip
The same SNP reported from the opposite DNA strand (A/G becomes T/C)


Switch error
A place where an estimated haplotype jumps from one true chromosome copy to the other; the switch error rate measures phasing accuracy


TDT
Transmission disequilibrium test: a family-based association test


Wahlund effect
Fewer heterozygotes than expected when separate populations are pooled

C.5 A note on originality
All explanations, worked examples, numbers, and figures in this guide were written and produced with originality using simulated and public datasets. Standard formulas (Hardy-Weinberg, F, D and r², the GRM, KING, λ, FST) and standard cut-offs (such as the KING relationship categories) are given with their original references. Where a teaching idea is shared with the courses listed above, those courses are acknowledged here and in the Welcome page.
